neighbours.name: Archbishop Gerhard II of Bremen
neighbours.summary: The oldest Saxon bishopric, founded in the eighth century when Charlemagne sent the missionary Willehad to the Saxons; the first church rose in 789 and a sizeable cathedral stands there now. The see moved here from Hamburg after the Wendish raids. St Ansgar, the Apostle of the North, lies buried here since 865. Archbishop Gerhard II contends with Bremen's independent-minded merchants for control of the city.

neighbours.name: Abbey of Corvey
neighbours.summary: A great scholarly abbey near Höxter, twenty miles east of Paderborn, where in the tenth century the monk Widukind wrote his history of the Saxons.

neighbours.name: Archbishopric of Magdeburg
neighbours.summary: Otto the Great founded a Benedictine monastery and the cathedral at Magdeburg and raised it to an archbishopric in 962. It has been the centre of missionary work and Church authority over the Eastern Marches ever since.

neighbours.name: Cathedral of St Liudger, Münster
neighbours.summary: Founded in 805 as a monastery, from which the city takes its name, to serve as a base for converting the Saxons. The cathedral is dedicated to St Liudger, its first bishop.

neighbours.name: Collegiate foundation of Quedlinburg
neighbours.summary: A foundation for noblewomen established by Mathilde, widow of Henry the Fowler. Its abbesses have ruled the town of Quedlinburg since.

neighbours.name: Schleswig
neighbours.summary: A fishing town on the north side of the Schlei fjord, grown up some two hundred years after the Vikings' Haithabu beside a Benedictine cloister of St Johannis. The earth ramparts and burial mounds of Haithabu, where the land crossing between the Baltic and the North Sea is shortest, lie a few miles off, and locals say its ghosts remain.

neighbours.name: Hamburg
neighbours.summary: A sizeable trading city on the Elbe estuary, founded early in the ninth century, destroyed by a Viking fleet in 845, burnt by the Poles in 1030 and raided twice by the Wends, after which its archbishop moved his see to Bremen. Frederick Barbarossa freed it of tax and customs on sea and river goods in 1189 and made it a Free Imperial City, but Valdemar II occupied it in 1216 and it now owes allegiance to Denmark. It controls the Lüneburg salt that Lübeck needs for its herring. If history holds, its free status returns in 1227.

neighbours.name: Nortorf
neighbours.summary: A small Holstein town where the roads to Schleswig, Lübeck and Hamburg meet. Unremarkable but for the small ash in its churchyard, cut down every New Year's Night by a white rider while a black rider fails to stop him.

neighbours.name: Lübeck
neighbours.summary: Germany's most important coastal port and one of its richest cities, the hub of Baltic trade, set on an oval island at the mouth of the Trave ringed by moat canals. Henry the Lion founded it in effect in 1157, built the harbour, made it a bishopric and granted the Statutes of Lübeck: self-rule by a merchants' council under an Älderman with its own justice, whose taxes pay for proud civic works, including a great brick cathedral at the south tip due within a decade. Furs, leather, timber, amber and iron ore come in; salt, spices, grain, herring, cloth and metalware go out, and a large fleet fishes off Scania under a profitable herring monopoly. Its merchants have kept a trading counter in Novgorod since 1205. The city has an ordinary Divine aura and is the home of Oculus Septentrionalis, of the Goldenes Kalb tavern and of the Novgorod Inn at the north end of town. Under Danish rule until 1227, when it is expected to become a Free Imperial City and, in time, the leading city of the Hanseatic League.

neighbours.name: Rostock
neighbours.summary: A growing Baltic port in Mecklenburg, overshadowed by Lübeck, and the chief town of the Sorbian princes of Mecklenburg. Valdemar I burnt it in 1161 and drove its Radegast-worshippers into the countryside, and it is now mostly German.

secrets.title: The Mecklenburgs' worship
secrets.text: The Mecklenburg family still worship Radegast in secret.

secrets.title: Storyguide Notes
secrets.text: See the Princes of Mecklenburg's record and the Cult of Radegast.

neighbours.name: Münster
neighbours.summary: A prosperous market city at the centre of the flat, highly fertile Münsterland in Westphalia. It grew from the monastery founded in 805 as a base for converting the Saxons, and its cathedral is St Liudger's.

neighbours.name: Dortmund
neighbours.summary: A Westphalian town known among those who know of such things as the principal seat of the Holy Vehm, the secret courts of the north.

neighbours.name: Paderborn
neighbours.summary: A Saxon town built round hundreds of tiny warm springs that form the source of the little River Pader. Here in 799 Charlemagne met Pope Leo III and the founding of the Holy Roman Empire was agreed; Charlemagne began a lofty cathedral and a palace for it, and the palace is now a ruin after fires in 1000 and 1165. The Externsteine stand on the edge of the Teutoburger Forest nearby, and the abbey of Corvey lies twenty miles east.

neighbours.name: Bremen
neighbours.summary: A port on the north bank of the Weser and the oldest Saxon bishopric, its first church built in 789 after Charlemagne sent Willehad to the Saxons; the see came here from Hamburg. The market traders have long held independent rights, and Archbishop Gerhard II contends with them for control of the city. The cursed, misted peat waste of the Teufelsmoor lies to the north-east.

neighbours.name: Lüneburg
neighbours.summary: A Saxon town built over extensive salt mines that have made it very rich, with grand brick buildings, though subsidence tilts the houses over rickety streets, and a planned great brick cathedral is of doubtful wisdom. Its salt goes out through Hamburg. The open Lüneburg Heath, where shepherds keep the goat-like Heidschnucken, lies to the south.

neighbours.name: Hildesheim
neighbours.summary: Called the jewel of northern Germany. In 815 Louis the Pious hung relics of the Virgin on a rosebush while hunting; they could not be removed, so he founded a church, and the rosebush still grows in a cloister by the cathedral. St Bernward, bishop early in the eleventh century and adviser to Otto II, established the Romanesque style here and left magnificent churches and civic buildings, artists and architects. The greatest church is St Michael on its own hill north of the cathedral, with six towers, many relics and paintings, and Bernward's crypt.

neighbours.name: Brunswick
neighbours.summary: Henry the Lion's residence in the twelfth century, adorned with art and monuments: the bronze Burglöwe lion stands in the central square, the fortress-like cathedral begun in 1173 is now complete and rich, in a style other Welf churches have copied, and beside it is Henry's fortress Burg Dankwarderode, named for the city's heroic founder.

neighbours.name: Goslar
neighbours.summary: A Free Imperial City on the northern edge of the Harz, famed for the Rammelsberg silver mines, Germany's largest and a prized imperial asset, now slowly flooding because spiteful gnomes have turned an underground river into them. Henry the Lion's claim to these mines led Barbarossa to strip him of his estates. Whoever drains the mines would be richly rewarded by the emperor.

neighbours.name: Quedlinburg
neighbours.summary: Henry the Fowler's effective capital for a generation early in the tenth century, with a castle on the Burgberg at the south end and a palace that has hosted Imperial Diets. The abbesses of the foundation for noblewomen that his widow Mathilde established have ruled the town since. It is now overshadowed by the greater Saxon cities.

neighbours.name: Magdeburg
neighbours.summary: Otto the Great's favoured city on the west bank of the Elbe, an archbishopric since 962 and the centre of Church authority over the Eastern Marches. The Magdeburg Law, with its generous charters and quick local courts, encourages new settlements in the east. The forgotten stone circle of the Teufelsküche lies deep in the Haldensleben Forest to the north-west.

neighbours.name: Louis IV, Landgrave of Thuringia
neighbours.summary: Louis IV, called the Pious, is landgrave of Thuringia, seated at the Wartburg near Eisenach, the ancestral castle founded in 1067 by Count Louis I and never breached. His father Hermann I, who ruled from 1190 to 1217, made it a famous court of literature and music on the French model, with lavish festivals and travelling minnesänger. Louis is to marry Elisabeth, daughter of the king of Hungary, who was raised amid the Wartburg's splendour and finds it empty, giving herself in secret to the poor and sick; stopped once with bread for beggars in her apron, she opened it to show roses. If history holds, Louis dies in 1227, Elisabeth founds a hospice at Marburg, dies in 1231 and is canonised in 1235, and the Teutonic Knights raise a great church over her hospice.

neighbours.name: Imperial Abbey of Hersfeld
neighbours.summary: One of the largest and most important abbeys in Germany, founded in the eighth century by Lullus, archbishop of Mainz. The springs it was built round are known for restorative powers of a magical kind; they and the giant bell in the Katharinenturm are both named for Lullus. Its rival Fulda lies forty miles south.

neighbours.name: Abbey of Fulda
neighbours.summary: The huge and wealthy monastery that holds the grave of St Boniface, the martyred English monk, and so a major place of pilgrimage. The Michaelskirche at the town's centre copies the Holy Sepulchre as a Greek cross, and four monastic churches outside the town at the compass points form a giant cross; the eastern one, the Peterskirche on its hill, holds the crypt of St Lioba, Boniface's kinswoman. It rivals Hersfeld.

neighbours.name: Bishop of Würzburg
neighbours.summary: A bishopric since the eighth century. The cathedral holds the shrine of St Kilian, the seventh-century Irish missionary and martyr who first brought the faith here and is popularly the patron of wine, for the bishop is master of Franconia's largest vineyards. He has begun a huge rectangular fortress on the Marienberg across the Main as his future residence.

neighbours.name: Cathedral of Bamberg
neighbours.summary: Emperor Henry II made Bamberg a bishopric in 1007 and founded the cathedral on the chief of its seven hills, where he is buried.

neighbours.name: Abbey of the Petersberg, Erfurt
neighbours.summary: The Benedictine abbey on Erfurt's Petersberg, where Barbarossa often held court. Erfurt's other hill, the Domhügel, carries the eighth-century Marienkirche.

neighbours.name: Eisenach
neighbours.summary: The town beneath the Wartburg, the landgraves' never-breached castle. Under Hermann I the castle became a centre of poetry and song; at the Sängerkrieg of 1204 Walther von der Vogelweide beat every rival, Wolfram von Eschenbach and Henry von Ofterdingen among them. Walther then wrote for Philip of Swabia and for Otto of Brunswick, helping the latter to the throne by 1209. The fashionable epics are the Nibelungenlied, made for the court of Passau, Tristan und Isold, Parzival and the Gudrunlied, beside courtly verse of chaste devotion to an unattainable lady.

neighbours.name: Erfurt
neighbours.summary: Thuringia's oldest and largest town, held by the archbishops of Mainz, from which St Boniface set out to the Slavs. It rises on two hills: the Domhügel with the eighth-century Marienkirche and the Petersberg with its Benedictine abbey. Frederick II's court has visited four times between 1214 and 1220. Its wealth comes from exporting woad for blue dye.

neighbours.name: Naumburg
neighbours.summary: A well-fortified, scenic town high above the Saale in eastern Thuringia, originally the New Castle the Ekkehardinger counts built when they moved their seat across the river in the tenth century. It has its own bishop and a prosperous market, and has just begun a large cathedral of St Peter and St Paul. The young and secretive sculptor-architect known as the Master of Naumburg, German-born, French-trained and rumoured to owe his unmatched work to sorcery or divine inspiration, is expected to leave great works here, at Mainz and at Meissen.

neighbours.name: Hersfeld
neighbours.summary: A town on the border of Thuringia and Hesse wholly dominated by its huge imperial abbey, whose springs are held to heal and whose giant bell hangs in the Katharinenturm.

neighbours.name: Fritzlar
neighbours.summary: A Hessian town. A little to the north, near Züschen, stands the Riesenstein, the stone the Devil threw at the church-building villagers of Neueburg and wept bloody tears on; the hidden glade of the Donar Oak at Geismar lies somewhere in the wilderness nearby.

neighbours.name: Frankfurt
neighbours.summary:
A city of some ten thousand on the Main whose bridge is the gateway between north and south Germany. Charlemagne founded it in the eighth century after a fog-hidden ford, shown by deer, saved his retreating army from the Saxons, and built a fortress on the Römerberg over an older Roman site. After the Treaty of Verdun in 843 it was the capital of Louis the German, who founded St Saviour's in 852; it declined in the eleventh century, and the Hohenstaufen revived and fortified it, so that it now hosts imperial elections. The Römerberg square holds markets, fairs, tournaments and coronation festivals, and Italian banking houses keep offices here. In 1220 Frederick II holds here his last German Diet for fifteen years.

On the road from Durenmar to the Gorge, between the Odenwald and Mainz, with a large market fair.

neighbours.name: Fulda
neighbours.summary: The pilgrimage town of St Boniface's grave, in a long valley between the bright wooded Vogelsberg to the west and the impenetrable Rhön to the east, laid out as a giant cross of churches round its wealthy abbey.

neighbours.name: Wimpfen
neighbours.summary: A favoured imperial residence high above the Neckar, held in turn by the Romans, the Franks and the bishops of Worms until Barbarossa took it in the twelfth century. The imperial palace stands where the Roman frontier fort had its temple of Mercury; the walls carry towers each of a different colour, the Roter Turm of red sandstone and the Blauer Turm of blue limestone among them. The bishop of Worms's administrator still lives in the grand Wormser Hof with much land and influence. The lower town clusters round the Stiftskirche and a Benedictine abbey by an ancient Neckar bridge, and the fertile wine hills of the Stromberg lie south.

neighbours.name: Neustadt an der grossen Linden
neighbours.summary: A free trading post in Franconia that has stayed a quiet backwater under its guardian lime tree, whose spirit has taken the townsfolk for its realm. The tree's siege-ruined branches rest on stone columns and monuments carved with the arms of the princes who fought there, and the townsfolk will not clear their woods. Prophecy says the town loses its freedom when the tree dies.

neighbours.name: Würzburg
neighbours.summary: An influential episcopal city of artists and scholars on the Main in central Franconia, amid the region's largest vineyards; wine is its export and St Kilian, whose shrine is in the cathedral, its patron. The bishop's new fortress rises on the Marienberg across the river. Peter von Würzburg of Fengheld takes his name from here.

neighbours.name: Bamberg
neighbours.summary: Henry II's city on seven hills, built from 1007 to rival Rome and far smaller, but keeping a spacious grandeur. Beer is its export: more than a dozen breweries, the oldest and largest of them the Bierhaus, older than the city and of legendary quality. East of it lie the weathered granite blocks of the Luisenburg and the empty Fichtelgebirge.

neighbours.name: Nuremberg
neighbours.summary: Among Franconia's youngest cities yet arguably its most important, home to the Kaiserburg on its sandstone hill, an unofficial capital and the Empire's treasury, where by custom each new emperor holds his first Diet. Barbarossa and lately Frederick II have added wings and towers, and the upper level of the Kaiserkapelle is for the emperor alone. A crossroads trading city exporting linen, with many carpenters who make looms. The Harberg, with its wandering Drudenbaum, overlooks it.

neighbours.name: Regensburg
neighbours.summary: The principal city of the Danube in Bavaria. The Rhine Tribunal's Bavarian lands stop at the river; Regensburg, the other Danube cities and everything south of it are claimed by the Greater Alps Tribunal.

neighbours.name: Mestwin I of Pomerania
neighbours.summary: Prince of Pomerania, a thinly peopled Slavic land between the Baltic and Poland that has been part of the Empire only since 1181, when Barbarossa made Bogislaw a duke. Mestwin rules under an oath of allegiance to Valdemar II of Denmark. He is old, with four sons; the eldest, Swantopolk, is expected to succeed him as duke. German settlers are arriving, the Church is weak here, and the Knights of the Sword found towns and monasteries and hunt pagan remnants in the forests.

neighbours.name: Albert II, Margrave of Brandenburg
neighbours.summary: Margrave of the low, forested march east of the Elbe that Albert the Bear, a Saxon, founded in 1150 after his campaigns against the Wends, and that his Ascanian descendants have ruled since. Its people are a thorough mix of Germans and Wends, and the forest is slowly being cleared for farms. Albert II is old; his heir is Otto, called the Pious.

neighbours.name: Dietrich the Oppressed, Margrave of Meissen
neighbours.summary: Wettin margrave of Meissen, a dynasty ruling since 1089, who also rules the march of Lusatia. Meissen is the most civilised part of the Marches, rolling, moderately peopled, fully German and a political and ecclesiastical backwater; Lusatia is forest wilderness peopled only by Sorbs. No Hermetic covenant has stood in Meissen since Sirmium fell to the Magyars in the tenth century, and the vis sources the Order knew there perished with it.

neighbours.name: Bishop Absalon of Roskilde
neighbours.summary: The Danish bishop of Roskilde who rode with Valdemar I's invasion of Rügen in 1168 and in 1169 destroyed the fortress-temple of Arkona, the holiest site of the sun-god Svantovit. The Danish Church brought the faith to the island, where it is still new.

neighbours.name: Cathedral of Brandenburg
neighbours.summary: The first bishopric east of the Elbe, founded in 948 by Otto the Great and briefly lost to a Slavic counter-attack later that century. Albert the Bear rebuilt the cathedral on the middle of Brandenburg's three islands.

neighbours.name: Marienkirche of Bergen
neighbours.summary: The church of Bergen, the only town on Rügen. With the Pfarrkirche at Altenkirchen it is one of the two churches of note on the island.

neighbours.name: Pfarrkirche of Altenkirchen
neighbours.summary: One of Rügen's two churches of note, on the windswept northern peninsula of Wittow, where two last priests of Svantovit scrape a living.

neighbours.name: Cistercian monastery of Rügen
neighbours.summary: A monastery founded after the Danish conquest of 1168. Its monks have only just begun farming the Mönchgut peninsula, which takes its new name from them, and a church is planned at Sagard, five miles from Crintera, which would push the Dominion toward the covenant.

neighbours.name: Bergen
neighbours.summary: The only town of any size on Rügen, founded by the Danes and ruled by them, with the Marienkirche. The islanders are mostly Slavic, Christianity is new, and the Danes have requisitioned every horse on the island.

neighbours.name: Stettin
neighbours.summary: A small port on the Oder below an old Wendish fortress, the ancestral seat of the Pomeranian rulers. Germans have settled since the middle of the twelfth century and paid for the church of St Jakob, finished in 1187.

neighbours.name: Brandenburg
neighbours.summary: The only notable city of the margravate east of the Elbe, on the site of an old Wendish settlement across three adjacent islands in the Havel; the middle island carries the cathedral Albert the Bear rebuilt.

neighbours.name: Meissen
neighbours.summary: Seat of the margravate, on the left bank of the Elbe below the Burgberg, the stronghold Henry I founded in 929. A bishopric since 963, with a prosperous market where German merchants meet traders from Lusatia, Silesia and Poland, but not yet rich enough for a cathedral. Upstream the limestone pinnacles of the Bastei rise a thousand feet over the river.

neighbours.name: Freiberg
neighbours.summary: The largest of the new mining towns of the Ore Mountains, founded in 1186 after silver and tin were found in that bleak evergreen range; a twelfth-century imperial decree lets anyone prospect there and keep the proceeds. Its merchants travel to Prague by the bridges at Most.

neighbours.name: Bautzen
neighbours.summary: The one place in Lusatia with real German influence, not far from Meissen. The Peace of Bautzen in 1018 ceded the area from Henry II to Boleslaus I of Poland, and it returned to the Empire in 1033. The Knights of the Sword keep a large fortification here where slaves, mostly Pomeranian, are held before being taken south to the market at Prague.

neighbours.name: King Otakar of Bohemia
neighbours.summary: Premyslid king of Bohemia, a semi-autonomous subject kingdom of the Empire that Barbarossa raised from a duchy a generation ago. His house has ruled since the eighth century, descended from the farmer Premysl whom the Gifted princess Libuse chose by vision at Vysehrad. The margrave of Moravia, the Empire's easternmost march on the Hungarian border, is usually the king's son or brother. Bohemia has no great cities, only modest towns round and north of Prague, living by farming, hunting, mining, glass, brewing and horses; many more towns are expected to be founded through the century as German feudal ways replace the Slavic chiefdoms.

neighbours.name: Basilica of St Vitus, Prague
neighbours.summary: The seat of the bishopric of Prague, created in 973 under Mainz with Thietmar of Merseburg as its first bishop. Inside the castle, it holds the shrine and grave of St Wenceslaus and relics of St Adalbert. The Basilica of St George, with its convent, stands beside it.

neighbours.name: Strahov monastery
neighbours.summary: An austere Premonstratensian house near Prague Castle, founded in 1140.

neighbours.name: Sedlec monastery
neighbours.summary: A Cistercian monastery a couple of dozen miles south-east of Prague, founded in 1142. A monk named Anton, napping after work in the vineyard, woke to find three rods of silver sprouting beside his head and left his frock, his kutna, to mark the spot; the monks have just opened a mine there of fantastically rich deposits. If history holds, a wealthy royal town grows up round it later in the century and takes Goslar's place as the Empire's chief source of silver. A far-sighted magus might buy the land for a trifle and mine it by magic, until Bohemian merchants notice prices rising and the Quaesitores take an interest.

neighbours.name: Prague
neighbours.summary: Bohemia's chief settlement and the ancestral seat of its rulers, founded late in the ninth century on the Vltava at the land's centre; small by German standards at about three thousand people. Prague Castle on its hill over the west bank encloses the basilicas of St George and St Vitus, with Strahov monastery nearby, and a second castle stands on Vysehrad rock just south. Since the eleventh century the city has spread to the east bank, with a market run mostly by German merchants and a small Jewish quarter. It exports cheap glassware to northern Germany and holds a large slave market.

neighbours.name: Most
neighbours.summary: A town and market south of the Ore Mountains, grown up round the maze of wooden bridges over swampy ground that lets merchants pass between Freiberg and Prague; its name means Bridge.

neighbours.name: Brünn
neighbours.summary: Seat of the Premyslid margraves of Moravia, where a castle and the church of St Michael were founded on Petrov Hill early in the eleventh century at the meeting of the Svitava and Svratka; a market town and mines have grown round them, and a handful of German settlers have lately arrived. In the town hall hangs the stuffed carcass of the Dragon of Brünn, which generations ago ate townsfolk from a cave by the Svratka until a travelling butcher fed it an ox hide sewn full of unslaked lime; it drank from the river and burst. Whether he was a butcher, a wizard or a magus in disguise nobody knows.

neighbours.name: The Hansas
neighbours.summary: Associations of merchants for mutual protection, the settling of disputes and agreed prices, which have existed since at least the twelfth century but remain small. If history holds, a treaty between Lübeck and Hamburg in 1241, sharing the cost of guarding the Trave and Elbe against robbers and punishing crimes against each other's burgesses, becomes the first great one; scores of German and Baltic cities join over the following decades, and by 1300 the League is rich and powerful under Lübeck's lead, fighting pirates with bigger ships, convoys, hired armies and noble allies. Whether Oculus Septentrionalis stands at its heart, and whether Imanitos Mendax plants corruption there, is for the storyguide.

details.wants: Protection from robbers and pirates; agreed prices; justice for their burgesses abroad
details.offers: Mutual protection, settlement of disputes and price agreements among member merchants

neighbours.name: The Holy Vehm
neighbours.summary: A system of secret courts, mainly in northern Germany and seated at Dortmund, claiming the power of life and death from an imperial mandate of Charlemagne. Its members, the Wissende, number tens of thousands: any free, legitimately born man who is neither excommunicate nor outlaw may be initiated. It works by secret meetings, kidnappings by night, hostile trials and in some regions torture, and passes one sentence, hanging in a public place with an SSGG knife left by the corpse. Its officers are the Stuhlherr, usually the local secular or church lord; the Freigraf, appointed for life, who truly rules the court; the Freischöffen who accuse and decide; the Fronboten who execute; and the Fehmenotes, secret informants across the Empire. Its supreme head is the archbishop of Cologne. Philippus Niger of Durenmar has assured House Guernicus that it poses no danger to the Order.
neighbours.ruler: The archbishop of Cologne, as Oberststuhlherr

details.rules: Members swear to uphold the Vehm, keep its secrets even from kin and report everything; each receives a rope and a knife marked SSGG. Courts sit on a hillock or known spot, lately also in vast underground chambers, and intruders are killed. An accused who does not appear is condemned if the accuser brings seven character witnesses, without the charge being examined; one who appears needs twenty-one to be acquitted; a member clears himself by oath unless charged with betraying the Vehm. Women, children, Jews, heathens and in practice nobles are exempt.
details.wants: The Blutbann, the power of life and death, which it says the nobility has usurped
details.offers: Judgement on heresy, witchcraft, perjury, murder and sacrilege where the lords will not act

secrets.title: Philippus Niger's men in the Vehm
secrets.text: Philippus Niger uses the Vehm: two of his trusted men are Freigrafs and he knows more than twenty Fehmenotes.

secrets.title: The Vehm's hangings
secrets.text: Philippus Niger has had dozens of suspected hedge wizards and at least one Marched magus hanged by the Vehm's courts, and is spreading it southward as a weapon against hedge wizards.

secrets.title: Philippus Niger's assurance
secrets.text: Philippus Niger has no grounds for his assurance to House Guernicus.

neighbours.name: The Witches of the Harz
neighbours.summary: Cunning-folk who venerate Walpurga as a goddess and keep the old ways with dozens of traditional villagers. They hold council on the Hexentanzplatz crag every April and go on to the Brocken on Walpurgis Night, 30 April, to light fires and sing to forgotten gods while Walpurga calls up the spirits of summer against winter's; only the most powerful may approach the Witches' Altar at the summit. Their design is left to the storyguide, as folk with minor powers of potion and charm; they can never cast true spells or work major magic, or the Order would long since have absorbed or destroyed them. Magi know the gatherings as a good place to find a potential apprentice.

details.rules: Council at the Hexentanzplatz each April; only the strongest approach the Witches' Altar
details.wants: To venerate Walpurga and keep the old ways of the villages
details.offers: Potions, charms and the goddess's favour; a place where magi find apprentices

neighbours.name: Priesthood of Woden
neighbours.summary: Tall red-bearded priests in long white cloaks who once came to the forgotten stone circle of the Teufelsküche, deep in the Haldensleben Forest north-west of Magdeburg, in the hour before dawn with men in skins and darker shapes, to slaughter a sacrifice and burn its vitals to herald the day. The missionaries who purged the cult named the place the Devil's Kitchen. Whether any of the priests survive is for the storyguide; the Wild Hunt rises from the same stones.

neighbours.name: Cult of Radegast
neighbours.summary: The worship of Radegast, the Slavic god of chieftainship and war, and also of fertility and harvest. His worship was anciently centred in Pomerania at his Oracle in the fortress-temple of Rethra, now ruined and plundered, though Mount Radhost in Moravia was always his sacred site and the Ex Miscellanea half of Roznov is his priesthood, with Igor Rastvan as high priest. His devotees are often tied to noble or royal pagan families and serve as court advisers; his favoured are inspiring and commanding, and overconfident. The princes of Mecklenburg were driven from his open worship in 1161.
neighbours.ruler: Igor Rastvan of Roznov, high priest

details.wants: A kingdom of the Slavs united under Radegast
details.offers: Temporal influence at pagan courts; the god's favour to the inspired and the overconfident

secrets.title: The Mecklenburgs at Rethra
secrets.text: The Mecklenburg nobility still come secretly to Rethra to honour Radegast and have gained powers from him.

secrets.title: A prophet of Radegast
secrets.text: Imanitos Mendax poses as Radegast's prophet to the Mecklenburgs.

secrets.title: The Roznov festival
secrets.text: At Roznov the summer-solstice festival hides human sacrifices.

secrets.title: Storyguide Notes
secrets.text: In the saga plot Between the Devil and the Deep Blue Sea, Radegast is a demon.

neighbours.name: Pirates of Frisia
neighbours.summary: The pirates of the Frisian coast, Waddenzee's among them, who bury their dead at the Pirates' Graveyards in Drenthe, a low ridge of standing stones and boulders above the swamp a couple of dozen miles up the Ems, the only stones in Friesland. The local nobility cannot unite against them.

neighbours.name: House Tremere in the Rhine
neighbours.summary: The Tremere of the Tribunal fall under two men. Stentorius of Fengheld is exarch and holds about three-fifths of the Tremere sigils, his filius's and the two Tremere of Triamore's among them; Severicus of Roznov holds the other two-fifths, including his two filii's and Hygwald Veritas's of Waddenzee. Fengheld's Tremere, with the Transylvanian Tribunal, served Henry III's conquests of Bohemia, Poland and Hungary and seized many vis sites; blocked by the Tribunal from founding daughter covenants, they built chapter houses instead, the largest run by Clemens filius Stentorius, and have lately loosened their Transylvanian ties. Roznov Fort remains an arch-conservative stronghold in regular contact with Transylvania, suspected since 1074 of being a beach-head for that Tribunal, and its companion Ladislaus sends Gifted children from the Prague slave market to Coeris.

details.rules: Only Stentorius and Severicus hold their own sigils; the exarch holds about three-fifths of the rest, Severicus the remainder
details.wants: Order, hierarchy and a strong hand on the Tribunal's eastern frontier

neighbours.name: The bear lineage of House Bjornaer
neighbours.summary: Bjornaer magi of bear heartbeast who look back to the Founder herself; the Senior Elder of the House always has a bear heartbeast in her memory.

secrets.title: Who is left of the line
secrets.text: An ancient hidden line descending from Bjornaer, now only Archmage Urgen of Crintera and his filia Odorpes of Fengheld's Lusatia chapter.

secrets.title: The Bears' Cave
secrets.text: Urgen and Odorpes keep the Bears' Cave in the northern Harz, floored with the bones of primeval bears, as a private source of Animal vis; each visits now and then and would be furious to find anyone else harvesting it.

neighbours.name: Harmonists of House Bjornaer
neighbours.summary: One of the two ancient factions of House Bjornaer, whose shared philosophy holds the Magic realm to be the pristine state of the world before the fae, who arise where wilderness mixes with human curiosity, and that wilderness must be guarded from mankind, the Church and the fae alike. Harmonists hold that human expansion cannot be stopped and Bjornaer are too few to defend everything, so mundanes who do not destroy the wild must be taught to live beside it. They dominate the council at Crintera: Jon Arnsson and Phyllia are committed, and Falke leans their way without declaring. Their counsel prevailed in 1168, when the House chose to wait out the Danes on Rügen.

details.rules: Dominant on the Bjornaer council; chose in 1168 to wait out the Danish occupation
details.wants: Mundanes persuaded to live respectfully alongside the wild

neighbours.name: Wilderists of House Bjornaer
neighbours.summary: The more extreme faction of House Bjornaer. Wilderists would keep humanity behind city walls and the wild places feared, and their zealots work to turn farmland back to wilderness and drive settlers off. Urgen, Senior Elder, former Primus and leader of the Hawthorn Gild, is their most influential voice, arguing that the Order must hold back the growing mundane population and that Bjornaer should enter Hermetic politics to do it; Istvan Padas of the Horse seat belongs, and Zora, priestess of Hertha, backs them. They gain adherents as the occupation of Rügen drags on, and the Gathering of 1227 is expected to bring the dispute to a head.

details.rules: Zealots revert tamed land to wilderness and drive out settlers
details.wants: Humans confined to walled cities; forests, marshes and moors left to beasts and feared

secrets.title: Urgen's campaigns
secrets.text: Urgen is widely suspected of driving mundanes from the wild with covert animal attacks, and is stepping up such campaigns now he is free of the Primacy.

neighbours.name: Volkhvy of the Forest Brothers
neighbours.summary: The few remaining priests of Rugevit, Porevit and Porenitz, the gods of rowan, beech and larch still worshipped in Rügen's wild places. They are welcome in the Stubnitz Forest, bury devout believers among the graves and megaliths of the Ziegensteine near Mönchgut, and alone can open the great empty barrow there, which they often let Bjornaer magi use because of their friendship with Crintera; Janis, leader of Crintera's Swan clan, is one of them.

details.rules: All male; nearly all have Ways of the Forest and a fierce devotion to family
details.offers: Burial at the Ziegensteine; the opening of its gate for Bjornaer magi

secrets.title: The barrow's gateway
secrets.text: The barrow at the Ziegensteine is a pre-Hermetic gateway, one end of a faerie trod through a particularly dark region of Arcadia that comes out near the covenant of Pripet Major in the Novgorod Tribunal. Nobody at the Russian end can open it, so it works one way only.

neighbours.name: Volkhvy of Svantovit
neighbours.summary: Only two priests of the four-faced sun- and war-god Svantovit remain, a very old man and his grandson, scraping a living on the windswept Wittow peninsula below the ruined temple of Arkona that Bishop Absalon destroyed in 1169. The elder is trying to pass on all he knows; the grandson has seen no power and follows only out of family duty. No white horse remains on Rügen for the Great Ritual, since the Danes took them all; were one brought, the old man would have his grandson steal it, and the rite's display of power would make the doubter a zealous pagan messiah bent on returning Rügen to the god, which watching magi might take for diabolism.

details.wants: A white horse for a Great Ritual to the four-faced god
details.offers: Knowledge of the rites of Arkona, which helped Falke learn to thaw the Baltic

secrets.title: Svantovit's statue
secrets.text: The two priests of Svantovit have laboriously moved the surviving upper half of Svantovit's statue from Arkona into a well-hidden shrine: four faces looking four ways, a bull's horn in its right hand, the god's huge sword laid before it. Looters took the jewelled saddle and bridle.

neighbours.name: Priesthood of Hertha
neighbours.summary: A small priesthood of women led by Zora, darkly beautiful through her goddess's gifts and the lover of Istvan Padas of Crintera, whose Wilderist stance she strongly backs. Every Walpurgis Night Hertha bathes in the small dark lake in the Stubnitz Forest a short walk from Crintera and afterwards drowns one of the mortals gathered to watch, marked by the priestess and the only one present unaware of his fate; the ghosts of earlier victims gather on the shore. Crintera protects the priestesses from discovery, and in return Zora gives the covenant Creo vis each year and never chooses her victim from its covenfolk.

details.rules: Every May Eve the goddess bathes in Hertha Lake and one marked watcher is drowned
details.offers: Good harvests for farmers who sprinkle their field corners with the lake's water; Creo vis yearly to Crintera

neighbours.name: The Order of Odin
neighbours.summary:
The Norse wizards beyond the northern border, as the Order imagines them. The fear of them has stopped any Hermetic covenant lasting long enough in Norse lands to attend a Tribunal, which leaves Zealand a grey area between the Rhine and Novgorod. The Tribunal founded Oculus Septentrionalis in 1144 to learn about them and it never did; the new covenant of Heorot has taken up the task, and Pancrestis of Heorot longs to meet a Norse wizard. Most Lowland magi know of at least a few Scandinavian wizards.

Whether it exists at all the book leaves to the storyguide, who must answer two questions: are there Norse wonder-workers who can match a Hermetic magus, and is there any organisation among them, and how tight? The answer may run from a Norse mirror of the Order hurling runic spells down to scattered weak hedge wizards brewing love potions. Norse legend tells of magicians who change shape, foretell the future and see far places, and of some who use runes to raise the dead, rule the weather, aid in battle and curse their foes; no single one of them should do all of these.

Waddenzee hunts Norse wizards on the Ash Gild's behalf and has killed a handful; Heorot studies them; Oculus Septentrionalis wants the Baltic trade.

details.wants: Undecided: a rival Order's dominion over the North, or nothing more than a hedge wizard's living
details.offers: Norse magics of shape-changing, prophecy, far-seeing and the runes

secrets.title: Waddenzee and the myth
secrets.text: Waddenzee has found no evidence of an organised Order of Odin and keeps the myth alive anyway.

secrets.title: Storyguide Notes
secrets.text: The bulk of any such order may be Gymir's wizard pawns, or renegade Hermetic magi.

neighbours.name: The Knights of the Sword
neighbours.summary: A military order founded in 1202 by Albert von Buxhövden, bishop of Riga, to crusade against the pagans of Livonia, far east along the Baltic in the Novgorod Tribunal; they took Fellin in 1211, massacring captives and baptising by force, and it is now their base. They grow ever more lawless, in an uneasy alliance with the Danish king and with Bishop Albert, who cannot restrain them. In Pomerania their war is as good as won and knights have settled on seized estates, feared by all and most by the less pious; nearly twenty years ago they desecrated and looted the temple of Rethra. They control the slave trade, holding slaves, mostly Pomeranian, at their fortification in Bautzen before taking them to Prague, and the profits fund their expansion.
neighbours.ruler: Albert von Buxhövden, bishop of Riga, founder

details.rules: A rule modelled on the Templars; in practice murder, rape and robbery go unpunished
details.wants: The pagan Baltic conquered and baptised; estates and silver
details.offers: Christian towns and monasteries in Pomerania; slaves for the Prague market

neighbours.name: The Werewolves of Pomerania
neighbours.summary: The fireside tales of witches and werewolves in the Eastern Marches are warnings, and villagers watch neighbours and strangers for odd features or accents, for animals' fear, for a prickling neck. Shapeshifting runs in distinct lineages that form one far-flung extended family, passed reliably from two werewolf parents and less so from one; some live apart from humanity, others prey on livestock and children. Their only organisation, contrary to what House Bjornaer believes, is the yearly meeting on 30 April where disputes are settled, territories agreed, kinships renewed and the young hear the legends of a glorious past united under a war-leader against the Romans. Children of werewolf families are Skinchangers; those born to human families usually have the Lycanthrope Flaw and cannot control the change. Small animals flee them, horses shy and dogs bark, unless they have Animal Ken. Some, especially women, become greatly respected witches with powers of entrancement or second sight. The storyguide may add bear or lynx clans.

details.rules: Once a year on Walpurgis Night the factions of a region meet round great bonfires under compacts that forbid fighting
details.wants: Territory, kinship renewed, and the old glory remembered

secrets.title: The betrayal of Bjornaer
secrets.text: The Pomeranian werewolves' legends tell of the betrayal of Bjornaer, who carried their secrets to the Roman priests, which they blame for their fall from kings of men to fringe-dwellers.

secrets.title: What the Founder was
secrets.text: Bjornaer the Founder was a Pomeranian shapeshifter-witch of their kind.

neighbours.name: The God of Truth
neighbours.summary: A dualist faith that has arisen in the last decade in the villages near the Bohemian Forest. It teaches that a God of Truth made the cosmos, while a God of Law made and rules the material world without caring for its people, and that the Church errs by worshipping the stern God of Law. The God of Truth is immaterial and can be found only in the wild, where he has sent his angels, whom men call faeries, to guide humanity. With no clear leader or line of transmission, churchmen cannot stamp it out. Tales speak of the Prophet Iacob, always accompanied by an albino crow, who appears unpredictably and never preaches, yet the religion springs up wherever he has been seen.

details.rules: No catechism beyond reverence for the wild and leaving the churches
details.wants: Mankind led into the wild by the angels men call faeries

secrets.title: Who the Prophet is
secrets.text: The Prophet is Iacob of Irencillia, whose caricature Nestor is the white crow, carrying out Primus Handri's plan to found a religion in the name of the fae. The Quaesitores would be appalled.

neighbours.name: Waddenzee's piracy
neighbours.summary: Five magically enhanced ships and nearly two hundred pirates raid North Sea shipping from Terschelling, breaking mundane law daily and skirting the Code by leaving no witnesses. Oculus Septentrionalis has lost several ships and cargoes, the Nebelkönigin with its vis and books among them, and waits for one misstep; the Quaesitores have warned the pirates repeatedly that they will get no Tribunal support if the mundane authorities move against them. Only the nobles' failure to unite has saved the covenant so far.

details.antagonist: The magi of Waddenzee

stages.title: Ships lost
stages.clues: Merchants of Lübeck and the Frisian coast count their losses; a stolen flagship sails under a new master.
stages.ignored: The raids grow bolder and each pirate magus edges nearer a charge of High Crimes.
stages.stopped: A ship recovered or a witness left alive gives Oculus Septentrionalis its case at Tribunal.

stages.title: The nobles unite
stages.clues: Lords who could never agree begin to talk of the haunted island.
stages.ignored: A mundane army is raised against Terschelling, perhaps at Oculus Septentrionalis's secret prompting.
stages.turned: The Tribunal is asked whether Waddenzee's magi brought ruin on themselves.

stages.title: War on the pirates
stages.clues: Bigger ships sail in convoy; the merchant towns hire soldiers and court noble allies.
stages.ignored: With Oculus Septentrionalis at the head of the merchant league, a direct assault on Waddenzee follows; but this lies more than twenty years off.

neighbours.name: The Ash of Nortorf
neighbours.summary: A small ash seedling in Nortorf's churchyard, cut down every New Year's Night by a white rider on a white horse while a black rider on a black horse tries and fails to stop him. Prophecy says that one day the black rider wins, the shoot grows into a tree, and when a horse can be tied beneath it a king comes with a great army; while his horse stays under the tree he cannot be beaten and gains fell powers. The tree spirit is Infernal, of Might 10 now and potentially 40, ambitious, and able to grant victory and the gifts of entrancement, inspiration and toughness; the white rider is Divine, the black an agent of Hell.

details.antagonist: The black horseman and the spirit of the ash

stages.title: A tip about a vis source
stages.clues: Agents of the black rider tell the magi of a tree in a churchyard that will one day yield vis, but not of the prophecy.
stages.ignored: The characters are expected at Nortorf on New Year's Night to guard it.

stages.title: New Year's Night
stages.clues: A white rider comes to cut down a seedling; a black rider rides against him.
stages.ignored: If the Divine rider is driven off or killed he never returns, and evil gains a foothold.
stages.stopped: The white rider cuts the ash as every year, and the seedling stays small.

stages.title: The tree grows
stages.clues: The ash leafs and thickens year on year until a horse can be tied beneath it.
stages.ignored: A king comes with a great army and the tree's fell gifts.

neighbours.name: Boglins
neighbours.summary: Tentacled spirit-beasts of the northern bogs, Magic Might 25 of Aquam: eight slimy dark-brown tentacles twelve feet long round a carapaced sac of a body with a toothy maw, lying under murky water where a foul stench and faint murmuring betray their pools. Gluttonous, reclusive and cunning, a boglin ambushes anything that passes, chokes it with a cloud of stinking gas, paralyses it with venomous barbs and drags it to the maw within a few rounds to eat later. Each tentacle takes wounds separately and regrows over a season's hibernation; the carcass yields eight pawns of Animal vis, one per tentacle, and six of Perdo from the black nodule of its brain.

details.antagonist: Boglins, swamp spirit-beasts of Might 25

neighbours.name: The Holy Vehm's hangings
neighbours.summary: The secret courts of the north hang suspected witches and heretics after trials no accused can win, and leave an SSGG knife by the corpse. Their informants are everywhere, their jurisdiction covers witchcraft and sacrilege, and their courts have lately begun to sit south of their old lands.

details.antagonist: The Holy Vehm, and Philippus Niger behind it

stages.title: Courts in the south
stages.clues: Hanged men with knives beside them appear where the Vehm never sat before; a hillock gathering by night.
stages.ignored: Cunning-folk and hedge wizards near the covenant vanish one by one.

stages.title: A hedge wizard hanged
stages.clues: A wise-woman the covenant dealt with is found hanging in the market place.
stages.ignored: Informants note the covenant's own dealings; a grog or companion is summoned to appear.
stages.stopped: A Freigraf's men are exposed, and someone asks who he answers to.

stages.title: A magus accused
stages.clues: Seven witnesses are ready to swear; the accused is not expected to appear.
stages.ignored: A sentence of hanging on a magus, and a quarrel at Tribunal over whether the Vehm is a mundane matter.
stages.turned: The trail leads to Durenmar's archmage and a scandal before the Quaesitores.

secrets.title: Philippus Niger and the Vehm
secrets.text: Philippus Niger of Durenmar turns the Vehm on hedge wizards, has had at least one Marched magus hanged by it, and spreads it southward while telling House Guernicus it is no threat to the Order.

neighbours.name: Imanitos Mendax
neighbours.summary: A master of House Jerbiton at Oculus Septentrionalis in Lübeck who poses as the owner of the upmarket Goldenes Kalb tavern, with a discreet brothel upstairs for rich clients, and whose third trade is the blackmail and extortion of citizens and magi. Tall, lean and handsome, a subtle Mentem specialist with competent Imaginem for disguises; his covenant-mates find him useful despite his morals.

details.antagonist: Imanitos Mendax of Jerbiton

stages.title: Word reaches the pirates
stages.clues: Waddenzee's ships always know where the richest Lübeck cargo sails; airy spirits are seen about the Goldenes Kalb.
stages.ignored: More ships are lost and Oculus Septentrionalis blames bad luck.

stages.title: The prophet of Radegast
stages.clues: The Mecklenburg princes grow bold; a stranger is honoured at their secret rites.
stages.ignored: A pagan house with unnatural powers gains a Hermetic adviser.
stages.stopped: The prophet unmasked, the Mecklenburgs turn on their god's false servant or on the Order.

stages.title: Tainted stones
stages.clues: Greed and quarrels grow in the covenant's laboratories.
stages.ignored: The three magestones are copies; the Hermetic books Waddenzee stole are tainted, and Lucas von Beck's necromancy draws on infernal lore unknowing.
stages.turned: His treachery proven, Imanitos is expelled and the richest covenant in the Rhine has a new enemy.

secrets.title: Imanitos and the pirates
secrets.text: Imanitos Mendax feeds Eric Ribecus of Waddenzee advance word of the covenant's ship movements for a share of the plunder, perhaps by tiny Astasian messenger demons taken for airy spirits; discovery would mean expulsion and undying enmity.

secrets.title: Storyguide Notes
secrets.text: Optionally he is a diabolist of a hidden dark Jerbiton lineage serving the demon Radegast, corrupting Lübeck's notables through the Goldenes Kalb, posing as the prophet of Radegast to the Mecklenburgs, able to swap the covenant's three Verditius magestones for infernally tainted copies, and perhaps planting corruption at the heart of the coming merchant league.

neighbours.name: The Wild Hunt
neighbours.summary: Folk memory confuses two hunts. Hellequin's Hunt is a host of the unfulfilled dead in a mobile regio centred on Hellequin, a cursed spirit whose task is to guide souls that cannot reach Heaven; its ghosts seek the grace of mortals to pass on. The Wild Hunt proper is a troupe of winter and storm faeries that rises from the Teufelsküche and sweeps Germany on stormy winter nights: the Huntsman, a grim figure on an immense black horse in a storm-grey robe with a gleaming helm and a spear, perhaps a fragment of Woden, with ten to fifteen ghostly Horsemen of Might 20 who merge with their mounts and command fear, wind and cold, and twenty-five to thirty immense grey Hounds of Might 10 whose howls are the arctic wind. It hunts the Holzfrauen, holding that if every vegetation faerie is caught spring cannot come, and sometimes mortals; being spirits of wind and night it can only terrify, buffet and chill, unless the Huntsman talks a mortal into riding with it. Then every huntsman strikes with lethal force, and the rider is found at dawn exhausted and frozen, Enfeebled for good.

details.antagonist: The Wild Huntsman, Unseelie lord of Might 50

stages.title: Frau Holle's flight
stages.clues: For nine days before Walpurgis Night a humble wood-wife in a rickety wagon begs villagers for help and shelter and checks their housekeeping, the Hunt at her heels.
stages.ignored: A village that turns her away hears the Hunt pass over; one that shelters her draws its attention.
stages.turned: A peasant who carves her a new linchpin finds the shavings turned to gold; a farmer who hides her in his barn finds gold in his rye.

stages.title: Walpurgis Night
stages.clues: The Harz witches climb the Brocken, fires are lit on the slopes and the auras double.
stages.ignored: The Hunt fights the airy spirits of summer round the Witches' Altar and loses, and at dawn Walpurga drives her wagon off across the clouds.

stages.title: Stormy winter nights
stages.clues: Howling like the arctic wind over the peasants' roofs; a grim rider who asks a traveller to mount up.
stages.ignored: A mortal who rides is found at dawn, never to recover.
stages.stopped: A Holzfrau sheltered or a rider refused, and winter loosens its grip a little.

neighbours.name: Bandits of the Bergstrasse
neighbours.summary: Bandits hide in the swampy, deserted east bank of the Rhine along the western edge of the Odenwald and prey on the merchants who use the old Roman road, now the busy Bergstrasse, north to Frankfurt. Fortified way-stations are being built along the road against them.

details.antagonist: Outlaws of the Rhine marshes

neighbours.name: Fengheld's hidden ambition
neighbours.summary: Fengheld commands more than forty Tribunal votes, nearly a quarter of the whole, though they are seldom all cast together, and presents itself as the Tribunal's neutral peacemaker and arbiter of disputes. The more paranoid magi already suspect a hidden agenda behind the neutrality.

details.antagonist: The senior magi of Fengheld

secrets.title: Fengheld's real policy
secrets.text: Fengheld's real policy is to keep every other covenant so tangled in politics that nobody notices its own growing power, and it has worked so far.

neighbours.name: Balastor's liberation
neighbours.summary: A young journeyman of Fengheld, born feral, who believes enlightenment means casting off humanity and means to return himself and others, consenting or not, to a primal state. His magic releases suppressed emotion and behaviour, his face takes a savage cast when he casts, and he delights in humbling self-important mundanes.

details.antagonist: Balastor of Criamon

neighbours.name: The Great Khan
neighbours.summary: At the foot of the tallest peak of the Kyffhäuser stands a withered apple tree of Might 45, guarded by the unaging men-at-arms who failed to hang their shields on it. Whichever prince hangs his shield there rules all the West; Clovis, Charlemagne and Barbarossa each did and cut it down, and it regrows and withers with their fortunes. When it next leafs a terrible fight begins; when it fruits the king hangs his shield and the wicked are rooted out. The Mongol Khan may hear of it and come to hang his shield, and the fate of the West will turn on who stops him.

details.antagonist: The Mongol Khan

stages.title: The tree leafs
stages.clues: Travellers in the Kyffhäuser report the dead apple tree in full leaf.
stages.ignored: A terrible fight begins, as the legend says.

stages.title: The Khan rides west
stages.clues: Word from the east of a lord of horsemen who asks after a tree where kings hang their shields.
stages.ignored: The Khan's host reaches the hills and the men-at-arms meet it.
stages.stopped: Whoever defeats the guards and fails to hang his shield is possessed and joins them.

stages.title: The tree fruits
stages.clues: Fruit on the branches for the first time since Barbarossa.
stages.ignored: A king hangs his shield, all men rally to it, and the wicked are rooted out, whoever he is.

neighbours.name: Grendel's kin
neighbours.summary: Trolls still haunt the bogs of Zealand round the site of Hrothgar's hall, where the new covenant of Heorot has settled. They have killed fourteen of its grogs and taken the left arm of its leader Signum Irruptus, who believes them the degenerate descendants of gods and pursues his study of them regardless.

details.antagonist: The trolls of Zealand's bogs

neighbours.name: The Danish occupation of Rügen
neighbours.summary: Since Valdemar I and Bishop Absalon took the island in 1168, Rügen has had Danish rulers, the Danish-founded town of Bergen, new churches at Bergen and Altenkirchen, a Cistercian monastery whose monks now farm Mönchgut, and a church planned at Sagard, five miles from Crintera. The domus magna of House Bjornaer has been in Winter for fifty years because of it: recruiting a turb from an increasingly Christian island is hard, its magical resources were damaged, and the Dominion creeps toward the Stubnitz Forest. The Tribunal of 1186 split on whether the Guardians of the Forests ruling allowed a reprisal, and in 1194 Quaesitor Caecilius ruled that no wilderness had been invaded while Crintera's forest stood; the grievance drives the House toward the Wilderists.

details.antagonist: Valdemar II of Denmark and the Church on Rügen

stages.title: The church at Sagard
stages.clues: Masons and a priest arrive at Sagard; the monks' fields spread over Mönchgut.
stages.ignored: A Divine aura grows five miles from Crintera's regio and the covenfolk's children are baptised.
stages.stopped: Animal attacks and tales of witches drive the builders off, and Bjornaer magi face prosecution as after 1186.

stages.title: Crintera's turb dwindles
stages.clues: Empty roundhouses on the first level; the Horse clan's herd thinned by Danish requisitions.
stages.ignored: The Wilderists gain the council, and Urgen's covert campaigns grow open.
stages.turned: A Harmonist settlement with the Danes, if the Quaesitores and the king can both be satisfied.

stages.title: The Gathering of 1227
stages.clues: Fifty to a hundred Bjornaer converge on Rügen for the Teufelsjahr.
stages.ignored: The dispute between Harmonists and Wilderists comes to a head before the whole House.

neighbours.name: The slave trade of Prague
neighbours.summary: Prague holds a large slave market, and the word for a slave is the word for a Slav; the Church forbids only the enslavement of Christians. The Knights of the Sword control the trade, which pays for their corrupt expansion in Pomerania and beyond: they bring slaves to Prague and sell them to Jewish merchants who resell them in Muslim lands. An ordinary slave costs a few shillings, less than a good horse; the exceptional ten times that, and the young, healthy and strong fetch more. Owning slaves is legal in Germany and frowned on by the Church.

details.antagonist: The Knights of the Sword and the slave merchants of Prague

secrets.title: Who Ladislaus is
secrets.text: Ladislaus, a shady-looking man at the market, is a trusted companion of Roznov; he picks out Gifted children among the slaves, who are delivered to Coeris, the domus magna of House Tremere in Transylvania.

secrets.title: Where the other slaves go
secrets.text: The other slaves Ladislaus buys are traded or used by Roznov, and some become the victims of its summer-solstice sacrifices.

secrets.title: Storyguide Notes
secrets.text: Ladislaus has Magic Sensitivity.

neighbours.name: Giants of the Bohemian Forest
neighbours.summary: Giants haunt the Bohemian Forest, nearly as large as the Black Forest and kept free of men by its climate and its peat bogs, swamps and marshes. They gathered the great broken rocks of Obri Hrad, the Giants' Castle, on its hilltop above the Losenice at the forest's southern edge, and may still visit it, though its Magic aura of 3 makes it a possible covenant site. Rügen's giants were long ago driven out to Pomerania after an epic battle, leaving only the out-of-place boulders of that island.

details.antagonist: The giants of the forest

neighbours.name: The Rhine Gorge
neighbours.summary:
Below Mainz the valley closes in under forested hills. A poor road follows the banks at least as far as Bingen and Rüdesheim, but nearly everything travels by water, and in the middle, at the Loreley, the banks rise into cliffs. Between Bingen and Koblenz more than a dozen castles stand, with more a-building, because the narrow river lets a castle force a toll on the heavy traffic; the map is a chessboard on which nobles trade and conquer castles for their toll positions, and the worst of the minor lords levying 'unjust' tolls are plain robber-barons.

Only the greatest nobles, the archbishops among them, hold imperial leave to take a 'just' toll; the imperial rates are a penny for a small rowing boat of five or fewer, two for a large rowing boat or fishing vessel, four for a small ship of ten tons or less, eight for a single-masted ship and twelve for a ship of two masts or more. Two dozen vessels or more pass a station each day, so a station brings in ten shillings a day or better, enough to feed a couple of hundred peasants or keep a castle; but a toll needs real force behind it, and captains pass word of weak stations and run those that ask too much.

The river's two great hazards are the Bingen Hole and the Loreley rapids; nearly half the merchants carry their goods overland from Rüdesheim to Lorch to avoid the Hole, and some now as far as Kaub, where the count of Katzenelnbogen taxes them. Here the lands of the archbishops of Mainz, Cologne and Trier meet, and two ancient faerie courts face each other across the water; Trier's Roman remains lie up the Mosel and the Westerwald, where Siegfried slew Fafnir, to the east. Four covenants have stood here and all four have fallen, the last two so badly that the Tribunal of 1200 banned magic in the Gorge for twenty years. That ban has now run out.

secrets.title: The seventy-seven years
secrets.text: Students of the Tribunal's records notice that each lost covenant fell within exactly eleven Tribunals, seventy-seven years, of its founding: the root of the tale that the Gorge is cursed, officially idle speculation.

secrets.title: Storyguide Notes
secrets.text: By the middle of the century a dozen toll stations stand between Mainz and Cologne, and in the Interregnum of the 1250s they double in four years.

neighbours.name: Rüdesheim and the Brömserburg
neighbours.summary:
The site of Rudiaria, the first covenant of the Gorge, on the right bank opposite Bingen some twenty miles below Mainz. Rudiaria was founded in 892 with the First Tribunal's sponsorship and the grant of every magical site on the Rhine between Mainz and Cologne, a Flambeau-leaning house dogged by reports of malefic doings; a charge of diabolism against its magus Eginolf went unproven in 962, and in 969 the place burned in what looked like a magical catastrophe, every magus dead or missing, while a crippling famine gripped the region. Its lesson to later founders: do not deal with demons.

Nothing could be salvaged, and Archbishop Rudbrecht of Mainz claimed and sanctified the land. The magi's keep was rebuilt as the squat square Brömserburg, long held by a minor family of Mainz's vassals, and a sizeable village grew round it; the town's name probably comes from the covenant or the archbishop. Redcap Crumena's note of 1032 AA spoke of a fortress partly visible from Bingen with covenant boatmen at its dock; only the fortress is still true, hardly a trace of magic remains, and of the four sites this is the least promising.

The Brömsers have their own sorrow: Hans Brömser, taken on the Second Crusade, vowed his only daughter to the Church for his freedom; Mechthild, who loved a young knight of Bolanden, could not face the convent and drowned herself in the Rhine, and he built a chapel on the hill in her memory. Her restless ghost still troubles the family, and Thibaud the Fat, the present baron, quietly asks learned strangers for help.

secrets.title: Rudiaria's old dungeons
secrets.text: The old dungeons of Rudiaria beneath the castle were merely bricked up and forgotten, and may hold Hermetic treasures and traces of its black past.

secrets.title: A captive demon
secrets.text: Were the baron to open Rudiaria's old dungeons he might loose a captive demon on the district.

secrets.title: Storyguide Notes
secrets.text: Mechthild's ghost has no realm or Might given. In the Infernal reading of the curse Rudiaria sold its souls for seventy years of power, held Hatto II in thrall, tried to cheat and burned, and the famine and Hatto's madness both trace back to it.

neighbours.name: Rupertsberg
neighbours.summary: The hill above Bingen on which Hildegard founded her monastery in the middle of the twelfth century; it looks down on the town and on the Nahe's meeting with the Rhine.

neighbours.name: The Mäuseturm
neighbours.summary:
A slender half-ruined tower on a small island at the mouth of the Bingen Hole, built in the tenth century by the grasping Archbishop Hatto II of Mainz to squeeze tolls from the river. The tale runs that in a famine the starving begged him for his hoarded corn; he shut them in an empty barn and burned it, laughing that the mice were squeaking in his corn, whereupon thousands of mice poured out, chased his boat to the tower and ate him alive. Nobody lives there, sailors cross themselves as they pass, and none has landed in decades.

Hatto's shade still holds the tower: an Infernal spirit of Might 30 (Mentem), a ragged man-shaped shard of darkness with a twisted mitred face, wholly insubstantial and beyond any weapon, kept in being by hate (Hateful +6, Merciless +4, Brave +3, Int +1). It lurks unseen in the shadows (Perception and Awareness against 12, or 9 by day), fills up to ten people with a dread of the island that with repetition drives them mad or kills them with fright, the fate of anyone who spends a night there, and its chill touch (Initiative +3, Attack +6, dodged only with Brawl) takes a Fatigue level and gives it back five Might. Some ten swarms of demonic mice serve it, each of Might 10 (Animal), about a thousand mice to a swarm, fiery-toothed and proof against fire, and they grow back from the aura until it is cleansed. A swarm takes on about three people; an unprotected victim takes a stress die +6 each round, falling with better clothing and armour to -9 in full armour with helm and gauntlets (armour does not add its Soak), and kills ten mice for every five points of Brawl attack total; a swarm flees at half its number. Group or Room spells hit a swarm and its victims together; an Animal effect at Voice, Concentration and Group takes one swarm, and one more magnitude clears the island for a while. Hatto's crosier holds 6 pawns of Perdo vis, found only once he is destroyed.

secrets.title: Hatto and Rudiaria
secrets.text: Hatto's corruption and the famine may both be linked to Rudiaria's misdeeds.

secrets.title: Storyguide Notes
secrets.text: In the Infernal reading of the curse the covenant held him in its sway.

neighbours.name: The Bingen Hole
neighbours.summary: The stretch just below Bingen, one of the river's two deadliest: rocks, a sudden quickening of the current and treacherous eddies. Only skilled, seasoned or foolhardy boatmen attempt it, though there are enough of those; many merchants portage round it.

neighbours.name: The Stone of Bacchus
neighbours.summary:
A small wooded island opposite Baccharach's quay where the wildest part of the town's autumn-equinox wine festival takes place; a few yards off its far side a weathered finger of rock rises fifteen feet from the water, the Stone of Bacchus, touched by the locals for luck with the harvest. Far too small for a covenant.

Wine drunk on the island during the festival grants +6 to resist its ill effects, but brings on mounting hallucinations and visions and debauched behaviour that each reveller perceives differently (personality traits may shift by up to 3 for the night), and at dawn the drinker is at -6 for a day. The dregs left over are Muto vis, usually about 6 pawns and up to 12: the more riotous the revelry, the more vis, however much wine is left, and hoarding the wine does not help.

neighbours.name: Pfalz Island
neighbours.summary:
The site of Rheinstein, mid-river a couple of hundred yards above Kaub (not the haunted island by Bingen). Rheinstein was founded in 1123 by Schwall of Bjornaer and Fulmonious of Tytalus with the First Tribunal's sponsorship, promising every other covenant three pawns of vis a Tribunal for five Tribunals; its magi also seemed to hold Burg Rheinstein near Bingen, though they were seldom there, as Redcap Ioanna noted in 1265 AA. In 1200 an army of angry mundanes under the archbishop of Trier destroyed it, and the magi's fate is unknown; Horst of Mercere's report laid much of the blame on their own conduct, and the Tribunal banned magic in the Gorge for twenty years. Its lesson: be subtle enough and strong enough.

The island is about a hundred yards long and under half as wide. Its upstream half carries the castle, still unrepaired since the attack, with a tiny courtyard and the rocky stump of a central tower, and a small pier on half-sunk rocks facing the left bank where the traffic runs; the downstream half is a copse of a dozen trees, with a fresh corpse on a makeshift gallows. A longer, thinner, more wooded crescent of an island lies a couple of hundred yards upstream, joined by a spine of rock that shows only at the lowest water; at high water everything but the castle and the trees floods. It looks like a stone ship riding the river. Rebuilt, it would make a cramped but serviceable covenant and a uniquely good toll station, a bowshot covering the whole river.

Lord Robert Schönburg, the baron's bastard, holds it with about a dozen ruffians taking tolls that amount to piracy; Wolkan, a branded thief, is among them. Baron Jürgen Schönburg owns the island and must be dealt with. Dripstones (chalcedonius) grow on the rock spine, one a season, brownish and waxy to the touch; pierced and worn at the neck one lets its wearer see through magical or faerie illusions (Perception against 3 plus the illusion's magnitude) and tell truth from lies (Perception against 6), and each is worth a pawn of Imaginem; a passing captain may ask for the Loreley charm the old inhabitants sold. A young vine in the copse yields a little Intellego vis from its sap with great care.

secrets.title: Where the vine came from
secrets.text: The vine on Pfalz Island was cut in secret from Durenmar's famous vine; Durenmar does not know and may be displeased.

secrets.title: The dripstone charms
secrets.text: The old magi of Pfalz Island sold dripstone charms against the Loreley to ship captains.

secrets.title: The burial mounds
secrets.text: Two ancient burial mounds hide among the upstream island's trees; Robert Schönburg robbed them (paltry treasure, perhaps vis) and woke their guardians, two powerful undead corpses with powers of stealth and destruction, who wait for a midsummer night when the river is low enough to cross the spine and fall on the castle.

secrets.title: Storyguide Notes
secrets.text: The mounds' guardians are of unstated realm and Might.

neighbours.name: Loreley
neighbours.summary:
The narrowest and most treacherous point of the Gorge: the river squeezes into a canyon 150 yards wide roaring over hidden rocks between rocky slopes, and a cliff four hundred feet high, all but unclimbable from above or below, rises over it. Even with no siren singing (she may go unseen at night, in rain or in fog) the passage needs Profession: Boating against 9 from anyone who has not learned the rocks. Vis might be gathered here at great hazard.

The Loreley herself is a faerie of Might 30 (Aquam), an exceedingly beautiful maiden clothed only in the long golden hair she combs for ever with a jewelled comb (Pre +5, Com +5, Dex +2, Str -2, Sta -1; Hateful to Men +3, Jealous of Women +3). Daughter of the Rhine Spirit of the Rhinefalls, she resents mankind's taming of her father and wrecks its shipping, and envies women who win men's hearts: she lures mariners toward the cliff, climbs down, bends them to her will and drowns them. She has a faerie's nature (no fatigue, disease or ageing, speech with anyone, Second Sight) and a faerie's bane in iron, which wounds her at a touch. Her song (4 points, Imaginem) makes up to ten people a round long to reach her, an Intelligence stress roll against 9, with +3 for women and for wax-stopped ears, and a dripstone's wearer shrugs it off on Perception against 6; her gaze (8 points, Mentem) binds one man at a time who fails Intelligence against 12 to obey her utterly, even to death; she works any Creo or Rego Aquam effect up to level 30 for a point a magnitude; and for 10 points she melts into the Rhine, regaining 5 Might an hour and healing in minutes, hours and days, so that she is all but unkillable. Her blood holds 6 pawns of Aquam and her comb 4 of Imaginem.

neighbours.name: Kloster Maria Laach
neighbours.summary: A Benedictine abbey of 1093 in lonely meadows beside Laach Lake, the foremost monastery of the middle Rhine. Its church is a Romanesque masterpiece, the first columned basilica built with arches, and the garden court before it, full of statues and fountains, is a divinely inspired image of Eden; the aura of 4 is the garden's.

neighbours.name: The Teufelsloch
neighbours.summary: The Devil's Hole, in the hills west of Laach Lake: a huge eroded pit with steep crumbling edges, black within and of unknown depth, reeking of the livestock that have fallen in and rotted.

neighbours.name: Rolandseck and Nonnenwerth
neighbours.summary: On the left bank north of the Gorge the ruined castle of Rolandseck looks down on the quiet island of Nonnenwerth and its convent. Legend says Roland, count of Angers, Charlemagne's nephew and his greatest knight, loved Hildegunde, daughter of the local count Heribert, and began a castle and watchtower for them; called to fight the infidel in Iberia he was reported dead, she took the veil on the island, and when he came home too late the two could only greet each other across the water for the rest of their lives.

neighbours.name: Drachenfels
neighbours.summary:
The lowest of the Seven Hills and the nearest the Rhine, a thousand feet high. Under it runs the cave where Siegfried slew the dragon Fafnir and bathed in its blood to make himself invulnerable, as the Nibelungenlied tells; the catacombs are extensive and the aura of 3 runs throughout. It would suit a covenant were it not for Schloss Drachenfels, the archbishop of Cologne's great castle built directly above. Who or what lives in the caves is not said; perhaps Fafnir's brood endures, or that of his brother Regin who plotted the slaying with Siegfried.

The hills themselves have their legend: the wild Rhine once pooled into a lake here and spilled ruinously northward, until seven giants dug a gap with great spades to drain it, were paid in mined treasure, and left their spoil heaps as the Seven Hills.

neighbours.name: The Westerwald
neighbours.summary:
East of the right bank north of Koblenz, running more than fifty miles eastward with the Lahn valley for its southern edge: an almost unbroken rumpled blanket of birch, beech and oak with fir and pine on the heights, home to many wolf packs and, in its heart, to the faerie Court of Bright Winter. The count of Nassau, whose lands lie just to the south, is pushing into the forest and sending bands of foresters to kill its wolves.

The Court asks that the wolves be protected and intruders driven out, and would give leave to hunt and gather vis in return; the Rhine's ruling that magi may actively defend a wilderness applies. Red-Hame, a large faerie wolf of Might 12 with a ruddy ruff and back, carries the Court's wishes to the hedge wizards of Waldheim through his companion Torven. No aura is given for the forest as a whole; the glade at Waldheim is Magic 2.

neighbours.name: Waldheim
neighbours.summary:
The site of Oakdell, a dozen miles into the Westerwald. Oakdell was founded in 934 by magi of House Diedne with the First Tribunal's sponsorship and a ban on trespassing on Rudiaria's territory; unwelcoming and secretive, it brought spurious charges of spying against Durenmar in 997, saw Wizard War declared on its Caithlinn by Severus Maximus of Flambeau and on its Pietro by Cirion of Tremere in 1004, and was razed in the Schism War in 1016 with every magus slain. Its lesson: do not make powerful Hermetic enemies. Redcap Harundo's directions of 1075 AA still serve: by boat from Koblenz up the Lahn to Ems, north on the forest track for several miles to a weathered standing stone on the left, then a barely used path north-west for a couple of hours and over a small stream into a glade round an ancient oak.

The glade now holds a tiny hamlet of rude buildings and little more than a dozen people: the large hut of the elder Ludold, the smaller one of his son Torven, two more family huts and a barn. The crumbled foundations of Oakdell's two stone buildings hold a neat vegetable plot and an open pen of wild-looking pigs that obediently leave the vegetables alone. The villagers trade pigs for grain and see almost nobody else; visitors are met politely but warily. The path beyond leads toward the Court of Bright Winter, whom the villagers serve for protection while calling themselves the count of Nassau's loyal subjects and refusing to speak of the court.

Ludold, gaunt and white-haired with a necklace of bones, is a cunning man of minor potions and charms whose shelves hold bones, herbs, mushrooms and preserved organs, some perhaps vis, which he gathers round the glade; he will trade them for a wife found for Torven, there being nobody of marriageable age in the hamlet. A covenant could settle here by ousting the villagers, angering forest and court alike, or by living beside them, who resist any major building; the place is isolated and has nothing beyond the basics.

neighbours.name: The Courts of Dark Summer and Bright Winter
neighbours.summary:
Two rival faerie courts facing each other across the Gorge, their details left to the storyguide. Bright Winter, Seelie, belongs to light, snow, cold and the hunt, keeps court in the highest snowy hills of the central Westerwald east of the river, and is found at midwinter by day; Dark Summer, Unseelie, belongs to dark, fire, warmth and the fields, keeps court in the lowest swampy ground of the Hunsrück forest west of the Gorge, and is found at midsummer by night. Dark Summer rules Bright Winter from Walpurgis Night to All Hallows' Eve, and Bright Winter rules Dark Summer the rest of the year. With diplomacy either court might become a contested source of vis. Red-Hame the wolf serves Bright Winter; the Schönburg family carries Dark Summer's blood.

The storyguide may instead use the Courts of the Seasons of the forests chapter: King Holly of Winter in the Westerwald, the Alder Prince of Spring in the Odenwald, King Oak of Summer in the Palatinate Forest and the Willow Maiden of Autumn in the Hunsrück.

secrets.title: A cure for Karlotte
secrets.text: The fae of Dark Summer know a cure for Karlotte Schönburg and will sell it.

secrets.title: Storyguide Notes
