secrets.text: In the Faerie reading of the curse the two courts play a game of seventy-seven years with the Gorge's nobles as pawns and clear the board at the end of every round.

neighbours.name: The Schönburg
neighbours.summary: The large castle of Baron Jürgen Schönburg on the riverside hill just south of Oberwesel, on the left bank. The family descends at a distance from the fae of the Court of Dark Summer and keeps a little faerie blood, and a faint trace of Faerie hangs about the place at certain times of year. The red crocuses that bloom outside its walls in early summer are a source of Ignem vis. Here live the baron, his heir Karlotte, and, when he is not on Pfalz Island, his bastard son Robert.

neighbours.name: The Seven Maidens
neighbours.summary: Seven pointed rocks just breaking the water below Oberwesel, held up as a warning to Rhineland girls. Seven cold-hearted virgin sisters of the Schönburg, raised by a meek aunt after their father died of grief for want of a son, spent their days feasting, riding and hawking and toyed with and cruelly refused every suitor; pressed at last to choose, they left by boat, the eldest mocking the crowd on the shore, and a storm wave drowned them all at this spot.

neighbours.name: The Mosel Valley
neighbours.summary: The Mosel comes from the Vosges through Upper Lorraine, and its lower course between Trier and Koblenz winds between the Eifel and the Hunsrück past castles and south-facing vineyards. Smaller and quieter than the Rhine, it still carries fair traffic upstream from Koblenz to Trier or Metz.

neighbours.name: Treverorum
neighbours.summary:
The lost covenant beneath Trier, between the Fleischstrasse that leads to the main market and the poorer Niederstrasse behind it. First proposed in 1088 by Xantippes and Julia of Jerbiton and Selena Tibicena of Bonisagus to recover Rome's secrets, and refused for want of sponsors from Irencillia, Crintera and Dankmar, it was approved in 1095 when Arliandus of Tremere joined them. Mundane meddling ruined it: Redcap Ioanna was murdered in the city in 1151, Xantippes was convicted in 1158 of years of self-devised Mentem magic on Trier's people for gain, the covenant was fined fifty pawns in 1165 for harming the Order's standing with town and Church, and in 1172 Scholastus of Jerbiton declared himself its last survivor, called Trier unsafe for magi because of its churchmen, and left for the Greater Alps with part of the fine unpaid. Its lesson: do not meddle drastically with mundanes and the Church. Its symbol, the Porta Nigra, is carved on the smashed council table.

Redcap Ioanna's directions of 1236 AA named a merchant's shop on the Fleischstrasse and the password 'Pax Hermae'. The shop now sells wine under Isaac for his uncle David ben David, neither of whom knows of magi; the Blaue Keiler inn stands to its left and a narrow alley to a back street and a butcher's to its right. Two underground levels lie behind the shop under the alley, with five ways in: a bricked-off passage in the wine cellar that the last owner called haunted; the wooden ceiling shutters of two upper sancta under the rubbish-strewn old garden yard; a raised stone 'grave' of Selena Tibicena in the neglected graveyard across the alley, marked with a sanctum sign instead of a cross, hiding stairs to her sanctum (she is not buried there); a disused stair in a burnt-out house next to a brothel on the Niederstrasse, where vagabonds sleep; and, least likely, the Roman culvert from outside the walls, which runs a few hundred yards to the maze beneath the ruined Barbarathermen and the other way under the Frankenturm, a fortified merchant tower in the city.

Of the four sites this is the most intact and the most readily claimed, but it lies underground in a city: settling it without the merchant above knowing is nearly impossible, and privacy hard to come by. Its remaining vis is a few pawns of Mentem in old Roman coins in Arliandus's sanctum, and the ghosts of the amphitheatre outside the walls. Divine at street level, Magic 1 on the upper level and Magic 2 on the lower, as are many of Trier's other Roman cellars Magic 1.

levels.name: Upper level
levels.notes: Three sancta, decayed and mostly empty but for rubbish and rats; Selena's, under the graveyard, holds assorted skeletons. A wide circular light shaft at the centre, its path now overgrown and impassable, and an old ladder up.

levels.name: Lower level
levels.notes: The council chamber with its smashed oak table; a solid metal sanctum-marked door that reads as magical; the library of waterlogged, moss-covered books and parchment and the empty stores; double doors to an overgrown pond at the foot of the shaft and to the old sewer stream with the magi's burial alcoves. Behind the door Arliandus's sanctum stands intact: a well-equipped Mentem laboratory with modest treasures and Mentem vis in Roman coins. The Door of Deimos, iron embossed with faces and skulls inlaid in lead and silver, is unlocked but latched through a leering mouth: it compares whoever touches it with an arcane connection to the long-dead Arliandus (InCo 5, level 8, 6 a day, Touch, Momentary) and on a mismatch or a resisted check fills the intruder with terror (CrMe 15, level 43, Touch, Sun, 6 a day, Penetration 22, Intelligence against 12 or flee), gloves notwithstanding. The Crystal of a Hundred Candles in the ceiling lights the room when the door opens (CrIg 10, level 23, 24 a day). The Mirror of Dreams, gold-framed with smaller fragments, shows a willing gazer his thoughts as images and gives +3 to Mentem laboratory totals at a Warping Point a season (InCrMeIm 35, level 45, Eye, Concentration, unlimited). The Trumpet of Ghostly Summoning, a small silver trumpet, calls nearby ghosts and spirits and makes them visible (MuMeIm 40, level 41, Touch, Sun, Room, 2 a day). The storyguide may add books and laboratory texts here.

secrets.title: The ghosts of Treverorum
secrets.text: The ghosts of Treverorum's magi rest in the burial alcoves by the underground stream; disturbing one may bring pestering, or lost secrets at a price.

neighbours.name: The Amphitheatre of Trier
neighbours.summary:
A deserted oval Roman amphitheatre a few hundred yards east of Trier's walls along the Hermesstrasse, at the foot of the Martinsberg. Overgrown passages lead from the sandy arena into small empty chambers in the hillside once used by gladiators, where spells or Second Sight find faint ghosts; the arena is Magic 1 and the chambers Magic 2.

Three ghostly gladiators of Might 20 (Magic) linger: Marcus the Valiant, their leader, a stocky hoplomachus with round shield, arm-guard, greave, gladius and brimmed bronze helm (Str +2, Sta +3, Dex +3; Attack +14, Defence +13, Damage +7, Soak +7; Brave +3, Duty-Bound +3, Honourable +1); Cyrillus of Argentoratum, a wiry retiarius with trident, net, shoulder-guard and copper Poseidon mask (Qik +4; Initiative +7, Attack +12, Defence +14, Damage +7, the net a scuffling attack, Soak +4; Crafty +1); and Caudelix the Gaul, a burly giant of Size +1 with a great axe, iron skull-cap with a spectacled mask and leather breeches (Str +5, Sta +4; Attack +16, Defence +9, Damage +15, Soak +8; Violent +1). Blown here at night, the Trumpet of Ghostly Summoning raises the three, who arm themselves and challenge whoever is present to a duel to the death, each wagering a trinket of jewellery or Roman coin against a stake of like worth. The fight looks real but is not deadly: a killing blow knocks out, wounds are tracked as non-lethal and the players learn their true wounds only after treatment. A gladiator who wins takes his prize, later found buried in the chambers and ruined by age, and fades; one who loses fades leaving his trinket, worth 2 pawns of Mentem vis. Each fights once a year.

levels.name: The gladiators' chambers
levels.notes: Small empty rooms in the hillside off the arena's passages.

secrets.title: Storyguide Notes
secrets.text: The record of 1248 AA, Valdus of Tytalus fined a pawn for twice harvesting vis from Treverorum's site outside the walls, is the clue that leads to a vis source near Trier, and so to the amphitheatre, its ghosts and the trumpet.

neighbours.name: Fenistal
neighbours.summary: A regio deep in the southern Bohemian Forest, dangerously close to Irencillia, of which the Order knows nothing.

levels.name: The temple of Diana
levels.enter: The only level; with no intermediate levels, very hard to enter.
levels.notes: The exsules' hidden covenant.

secrets.title: What Fenistal is
secrets.text: Fenistal is the original temple of Diana, where Merinita served as the goddess's last disciple in Germania, long thought destroyed but held ever since by the surviving renegades of early House Merinita, the exsules, as their 'covenant'.

secrets.title: Fenistal's regio
secrets.text: Fenistal's regio has a single level, the top, with no intermediate levels, so that entering it is very hard; the strongest magic of its masters goes to keeping it hidden.

secrets.title: Who lives at Fenistal
secrets.text: Fewer than a dozen exsules live at Fenistal with the barest staff of servants, all once animals given human form, and two of them always stand guard.

secrets.title: What comes from Fenistal
secrets.text: From Fenistal come raids on weak covenants, the recruiting of failed apprentices, fae set against the Order, the Huntress in the Wood as an unwitting arm, and a long-planned revenge on the Tribunal.

secrets.title: Storyguide Notes
secrets.text: The regio's single level is at Magic 8.

neighbours.name: Louis I Wittelsbach, Count Palatine of the Rhine
neighbours.summary: Duke of Bavaria and Count Palatine of the Rhine. He holds Baccharach with Burg Stahleck, where his tolls are just, and Burg Thurant, and is overlord of Eberhard von Eppstein. A legitimate toll-gatherer, and, if the book's future holds, a member of the Rhine League.

neighbours.name: Werner IV, Count of Bolanden
neighbours.summary: A vassal of Mainz and a fervent builder of castles, with lands south-west of Mainz and Burg Ehrenfels, Burg Sterrenberg, whose tolls are unjust, and Burg Liebenstein. Elder brother of Philip I of Falkenstein. A knight of Bolanden was the lover of Mechthild Brömser.

neighbours.name: Dieter II, Count von Katzenelnbogen
neighbours.summary:
A fervent castle-builder holding a large, thinly peopled territory between the Taunus and the Lahn east of the Gorge: Kaub, whose tolls are unjust, Burg Hohenstein, Burg Kaub, still a-building, and Burg Katzenelnbogen, whose tolls are also unjust. His family rose fast from humble east-bank origins in two generations, and its castles and intrusion into the Gorge alarm the archbishops.

Tall, proud and not very pious, fond of tournaments and war, he loves nothing so much as ruthlessly gathering land and castles. Easy to make an enemy of, but treated with care and respect a possible ally: he has no qualms about dealing with useful wizards.

neighbours.name: Henry II the Rich, Count of Nassau
neighbours.summary: Holds land along the Lahn and round the Westerwald: Burg Nassau, the town of Nassau and Limburg, taking unjust tolls at both. He is pushing hard into the Westerwald to bring it under his hand and sends foresters to kill its wolves, the grievance of the Court of Bright Winter. Torven of Waldheim's uncle was one of his foresters.

neighbours.name: Gerlach IV, Count of Veldenz
neighbours.summary: A vassal of Trier whose lands lie south-west of Koblenz and along the Mosel.

neighbours.name: Eberhard II, Count of Aremberg
neighbours.summary: Holds lands on the edge of the Eifel west of Koblenz: Altenahr, Burg Are and Burg Aremberg.

neighbours.name: Philip I, Baron Falkenstein
neighbours.summary: Younger brother and vassal of the count of Bolanden, holding some of the Bolanden lands and Burg Reichenstein.

neighbours.name: Jürgen, Baron Schönburg
neighbours.summary:
Holds Oberwesel, the Schönburg and Burg Pfalz, where the tolls are unjust. Of distant faerie descent from the Court of Dark Summer. Father of Karlotte, his lawful heir, and of the bastard Robert, whom he put in charge of the Pfalz tolls; he is ashamed of Robert and suspects him of unjust tolls, but divided loyalties leave him paralysed and blind to the worst of it.

He owns Pfalz Island. Magi who cure Karlotte and prove Robert's guilt win his gratitude; he may then lease them the island, perhaps sharing the toll profits if they rebuild Burg Pfalz and run the station, though Robert's band must still be put out by force. Driving Robert out first makes an enemy of the baron.

neighbours.name: Eberhard von Eppstein, Baron of Braubach
neighbours.summary: A vassal of the Count Palatine holding Braubach and the Marksburg, where his tolls are unjust.

neighbours.name: Thibaud the Fat, Baron of Rüdesheim
neighbours.summary: A minor vassal of Mainz holding Rüdesheim and the Brömserburg, the old keep of Rudiaria. Haunted by the ghost of his ancestress Mechthild, he discreetly asks knowledgeable strangers for help.

neighbours.name: Arnold, Baron von Eltz
neighbours.summary: A minor noble holding Karden and Burg Eltz, where his tolls are unjust.

neighbours.name: Hermann von Wien, Baron of Sooneck
neighbours.summary: A minor noble holding Burg Sooneck, where his tolls are unjust.

neighbours.name: Bingen
neighbours.summary: At the southern end of the Gorge, where the Nahe meets the Rhine under a Roman bridge: an old walled town guarded by Burg Klopp, where tolls are taken for Mainz. The Bingen Hole lies just downstream, and Hildegard's monastery of Rupertsberg looks down on the town.

neighbours.name: Rüdesheim
neighbours.summary: A sizeable village on the right bank opposite Bingen, grown up round the Brömserburg and held by Thibaud the Fat, a minor vassal of Mainz. The overland portage to Lorch, and now to Kaub, starts here.

neighbours.name: Baccharach
neighbours.summary: A left-bank town amid wide vineyards making a potent and locally prized wine, with a modest quay. Its autumn-equinox wine festival draws townsfolk and peasants from miles about, the wildest of it on the island of the Stone of Bacchus opposite. Held by Louis I, the Count Palatine, from Burg Stahleck, whose tolls are just.

neighbours.name: Kaub
neighbours.summary: A walled town, little more than a prosperous village, on the right bank a couple of hundred yards below Pfalz Island. Count Dieter II von Katzenelnbogen took it lately, is building Burg Kaub on the hillside above, and has begun taking unjust tolls from the merchants who portage overland from Rüdesheim.

neighbours.name: Oberwesel
neighbours.summary: A prosperous left-bank town two miles below Kaub, held by Baron Jürgen Schönburg from his castle just to the south; the rocks of the Seven Maidens lie just downstream.

neighbours.name: Koblenz
neighbours.summary: A fair-sized city where the Mosel meets the Rhine, named from the Latin for the confluence. The Roman fort is long gone but the old walls stand; the chief church, the collegiate foundation of St Kastor of 830, has lately grown to four towers, and there are several more churches, a courthouse and many merchants grown rich on Mosel wine. Emperor Henry II gave it its charter in 1018 and the archbishops of Trier have held it since, taking just tolls. The Teutonic Knights have lately founded a chapter house at its north end.

neighbours.name: Limburg
neighbours.summary: A fortified town on the Lahn some two dozen miles above the Rhine, guarding a large wooden bridge of the twelfth century (not the duchy of the same name). Held by Henry II of Nassau, whose tolls here are unjust.
neighbours.ruler: Henry II the Rich, Count of Nassau

neighbours.name: The Teutonic Knights of Koblenz
neighbours.summary: A chapter house of the Teutonic Knights, newly founded at the north end of Koblenz.

neighbours.name: Kloster Maria Laach
neighbours.summary: The Benedictine abbey beside Laach Lake, founded in 1093 and the foremost monastery of the region, with its arched columned basilica and its garden court made in the image of Eden, where the Divine aura reaches 4.

neighbours.name: Rupertsberg monastery
neighbours.summary:
The Benedictine house Hildegard of Bingen founded on the hill above Bingen in the middle of the twelfth century. Hildegard, schooled at a monastery from the age of eight, was theologian, physician, mystic, diplomat, poet and politician, and most famous for music that seemed close to miraculous; she never quite mastered Latin and wrote through a scribe to emperors, popes and archbishops, and to several Hermetic magi. She had Communication +4 and was a Good Teacher.

Her works in the original are all of Quality 13 (copies may be poorer): Scivias, a tractatus on Theology; Liber Vitae Meritorum, a tractatus on moral Philosophiae and Theology; Liber Divinorum Operum, a summa on metaphysical Philosophiae at level 2 and Theology at level 5; Physica, a tractatus on natural Philosophiae and Medicine; Causae et Curae, a summa on natural Philosophiae at level 2 and Medicine at level 3; Ordo Virtutum, a tractatus on the music of Artes Liberales, moral Philosophiae and Theology; and Symphonia Armoniae Celestium Revelationum, a tractatus on the astronomy and music of Artes Liberales.

neighbours.name: The Curse of the Rhine Gorge
neighbours.summary:
After Treverorum and Rheinstein fell, the Tribunal of 1200 forbade all magic in the Gorge for twenty years. The ban has now lapsed, and Durenmar's leaders want a new covenant on the middle Rhine to put life back into a Tribunal where no covenant has been founded in decades, Fengheld's chapter houses multiply and magi drift away to other Tribunals. Newly Gauntleted magi, some who finished their apprenticeships at Durenmar and some invited from elsewhere, are to survey the four lost sites, choose one and found a covenant under Durenmar's sponsorship, subject to the other covenants' approval. Murion, Prima of Bonisagus and Praeco, lays out the grand but detail-light plan at the Forum straight after their initiation; Occultes of Durenmar may offer encouragement; Xavier of Mercere, the Tribunal's archivist, supplies the old Redcap directions, and a season in the Great Library yields the records of the four covenants.

The four teach the Lessons of Failure: Rudiaria, do not deal with demons; Oakdell, do not make powerful Hermetic enemies; Treverorum, do not meddle drastically with mundanes and Church; Rheinstein, be subtle and well defended. The storyguide may run it gently, with years of support from a parent covenant such as Fengheld or Durenmar and exploratory forays first, or throw the magi in at the deep end, with Durenmar disorganised and resources scant. The party should mix Rhine and non-Rhine magi: Rhine-trained ones may take the Gild Trained Virtue and a parens from the book's masters and archmagi; one or two from rich covenants start with a shield grog and money, and several, but fewer than half, should come from Fengheld with favoured resources for the sake of the politics. Grogs come from local recruits or sponsors' gifts, and a shield grog is played by someone other than its magus's player.

details.antagonist: The curse of the Gorge, whichever realm the storyguide gives it

stages.title: The Praeco's commission
stages.clues: Durenmar's unease is talked of: no new covenant in decades, Fengheld's chapters spreading, magi leaving. Right after the initiation at the Forum Murion names the Gorge, now free of its ban, and offers Durenmar's sponsorship. A season's work in the Great Library (a fitting Mercere Gauntlet) turns up the Tribunal records, and Xavier the archivist the Redcap directions of Crumena, Harundo and Ioanna. A side road: a panicked, injured young magus reports his reckless Jerbiton friend and their grogs dragged off by shadowy figures in the Black Forest, and Durenmar's own magi will not stir; the rescue may serve as a Flambeau, Tytalus or Merinita Gauntlet, may be a true accident or a parens's test, and the rescued magus may promise to sponsor the covenant.
stages.ignored: The magi scatter to other covenants or Tribunals and the Gorge stays empty; Fengheld may plant a chapter there instead.
stages.stopped: Murion is refused; Durenmar looks weaker still, and remembers.
stages.turned: The magi take the commission on their own terms, bargaining for gentle support or accepting the deep end.

stages.title: The road north
stages.clues: Nearly a hundred miles and about a week from Durenmar: the north-east edge of the Black Forest, Wimpfen, the Odenwald, where bandits waylay badly guarded travellers, Frankfurt's great market fair, and Mainz, whose archbishop rules the southern Gorge.
stages.ignored: A careless party loses goods or grogs to the Odenwald's bandits.
stages.stopped: The bandits are beaten off or bought; the magi reach Mainz intact.
stages.turned: A first acquaintance in Mainz or Frankfurt, a merchant or a cleric, becomes a contact for the years ahead.

stages.title: The four sites
stages.clues: At Rüdesheim only a fortress and a haunted baron; at Pfalz Island Robert Schönburg's ruffians, a corpse on the gallows and a cramped ruin that commands the river; at Waldheim a wary hamlet, tame pigs and a path toward the faerie court; under Trier a wine merchant's cellar, a false grave and a sealed Tremere door. Round them wait the Mouse Tower, the Loreley, the Stone of Bacchus and the amphitheatre's ghosts.
stages.ignored: Hatto's dread, the Loreley's song or Robert's gang take their toll of the unwary; a night on the Mäuseturm island kills.
stages.stopped: Each hazard faced yields something: Perdo vis from Hatto's crosier, dripstones against the Loreley, Mentem trinkets from the gladiators.
stages.turned: Thibaud, Ludold, David ben David or Baron Schönburg become friends rather than obstacles, each with a price.

stages.title: Forest or city, covenant or chapter
stages.clues: The choice mirrors the Tribunal's own divide: the forest covenants Crintera, Irencillia and Dankmar against the city covenants Oculus Septentrionalis, Triamore and Waddenzee. Durenmar wants a neutral traditionalist covenant to pull the Tribunal together; Fengheld wants a chapter house that would make it the Tribunal's giant, and makes generous offers at the cost of independence, which Fengheld-trained magi may favour.
stages.ignored: Drift leaves the magi with no site and no patron as Tribunal approaches.
stages.stopped: Fengheld's offer refused, Durenmar's sponsorship stands, and Fengheld becomes a rival, not an enemy.
stages.turned: A Fengheld chapter: funded and protected, bound by Fengheld's charter, needing no Tribunal vote, and Durenmar disappointed.

stages.title: Sponsors at Tribunal
stages.clues: A new covenant needs one sponsoring magus from every other covenant; one suffices against his fellows' views, and refusing reflects badly on a covenant, so modest terms usually serve unless the proposal looks like a direct threat. The deals are best struck in the days before Tribunal opens at Durenmar, and each sponsor brings a founding gift in the measure of its regard: books, items, valuables, grogs, some only promised. One gift may be an enigmatic item with only hints to its use; another's lavish gifts turn mundane and insulting when the Moon-duration Imaginem spells on them lapse, showing what the giver really thinks.
stages.ignored: Without a sponsor from every covenant the foundation is not recognised.
stages.stopped: A covenant that sees the Gorge foundation as a threat withholds its sponsor; the magi must find what it fears and buy it off.
stages.turned: The covenant is recognised, its sponsors' favours owed and their gifts in hand.

stages.title: Settling in
stages.clues: Mundane entanglement is certain: at the island, toll-gathering among archbishops, the Count Palatine, Katzenelnbogen and the robber-barons, with Robert's band to evict and Karlotte to cure; in the forest, survival, Nassau's foresters and the Court of Bright Winter's demands; under Trier, a hostile archbishop and a merchant overhead. Gild membership and the Durenmar-Fengheld rivalry pull at the magi from inside the Order.
stages.ignored: Unjust tolls, a slighted baron or a provoked court bring the fate of Rheinstein closer.
stages.stopped: The covenant holds its ground, pays or collects its tolls lawfully and keeps the Church at arm's length.
stages.turned: Katzenelnbogen or Schönburg becomes an ally; the Court sells leave to harvest vis; the covenant is a power on the river.

stages.title: The Lotharingian question
stages.clues: The north-western covenants, the Lotharingians, talk of seceding from the Rhine to deal more freely with mundanes. A Gorge covenant sits on the border and must choose between loyalty to Durenmar's traditions and a freer hand in a smaller Tribunal.
stages.ignored: Both sides count the covenant among the uncommitted and court or threaten it.
stages.stopped: The covenant stands with Durenmar and the motion fails or passes without it.
stages.turned: The covenant goes with the Lotharingians, and Durenmar's sponsorship sours.

stages.title: The seventy-seventh year
stages.clues: As the covenant nears its eleventh Tribunal the signs of its predecessors' falls return: malefic rumours and famine as at Rudiaria, powerful Hermetic enemies as at Oakdell, trouble with town and Church as at Treverorum, an army at the gates as at Rheinstein; the Rhine League, if history holds, is tearing down robber castles. The chosen cause shows its hand: the river spirit stirring, the Courts clearing their board, the devil of Rudiaria calling in its debt, or the Order's works withering where humble, pious wizards prosper.
stages.ignored: The covenant falls within seventy-seven years, like the four before it.
stages.stopped: The curse is broken at its root: the Rhinegold found and the river untamed, the game of the Courts ended, the devil defeated, or grace won through humility and the counsel of Albertus Magnus; the covenant endures as a lasting power.
stages.turned: The covenant survives by a bargain with the curse's source, and inherits its debt.

secrets.title: The seventy-seven years
secrets.text: Each lost covenant of the Gorge fell within exactly seventy-seven years of its founding.

secrets.title: The Magic reading
secrets.text: The curse's Magic cause, the revenge of the Nibelungs: Siegfried cheated the dwarves and giants who first tamed the Rhine, dooming his line and every kingdom or wise man who follows him to fall within seven decades, as the Burgundians fell to Attila, the Merovingians, and Charlemagne's empire to the Norse. Breaking it may uncover the lost Rhinegold and may require the untaming of the river's elemental spirit.

secrets.title: The Faerie reading
secrets.text: The curse's Faerie cause, the rivalry of the Courts: Dark Summer and Bright Winter play a game more than a thousand years old with the Gorge's nobles as pawns, and its rules clear the board every seventy-seven years, sweeping away nobles, covenants and kingdoms alike; the Romans were Dark Summer's pieces and the barbarians Bright Winter's, then Burgundians against Huns as the Nibelungenlied records.

secrets.title: The Infernal reading
secrets.text: The curse's Infernal cause, the pact of Rudiaria: the first covenant sold its souls to a powerful devil for gifts falling due after seventy years, grew mighty, held Archbishop Hatto II in thrall, and when payment came tried to cheat and was destroyed battling Hell in a great fire; the devil has since lured each later covenant to the same fall on the same schedule.

secrets.title: The Divine reading
secrets.text: The curse's Divine cause, the corruption of the Merovingians: the Christian wizard-kings, Merovech descended from David and keeper of the Grail, rose by God's plan and fell within seven decades to corruption and infighting; God blessed the Carolingians and cursed every wizard's work in the region to fail in the same span, the Order's included, and only humble pious wizards prosper. The counsel of Albertus Magnus may show the path.

secrets.title: Storyguide Notes
secrets.text: The saga can climax about seven decades in, when the curse's forces gather and the covenant meets its predecessors' fate unless it breaks the curse and founds a lasting Hermetic power. The storyguide chooses one cause, or none but self-inflicted misfortune. The Magic cause ties to Schwall of Bjornaer's schemes and the Path of the Heartbeast; the Infernal cause ties to the Gymir and Radegast arc. If history holds, the Rhine League of the 1250s is a further threat to any covenant taking tolls.

neighbours.name: Gymir
neighbours.summary: A name from the North that the Order does not know in 1220.

details.wants: (secret) the Church undone and the Holy Vehm turned on Radegast's followers
details.offers: (secret) storms, catastrophe and infernal power to its wizard pawns

secrets.title: Gymir's fief
secrets.text: A demon prince whose earthly fief is Scandinavia, at war with Radegast and with the Dominion.

secrets.title: Gymir's ways
secrets.text: Gymir strikes at the Church, works through catastrophe and weather and through the Norse, commands an aggressive faction of wizards, and profits from Waddenzee's piracy.

secrets.title: Gymir and the Holy Vehm
secrets.text: Gymir is worming into the Holy Vehm, meaning to turn the Vehm on Radegast's pagans in northern Germany.

secrets.title: Storyguide Notes
secrets.text: Might not given. Gymir has murdered the Vehm's leader, the archbishop of Cologne, in 1225 if the book's future holds.

neighbours.name: Radegast
neighbours.summary: A god of the Old Ways to the Slavs of the Baltic shore, as far as the Order knows.

details.wants: (secret) Germans turned north against the Norse, the Hansa corrupted by greed
details.offers: (secret) the powers of a 'god' to those who worship it

secrets.title: Radegast's fief
secrets.text: A demon prince whose fief is the Slavic lands, its heartland the eastern Baltic shore.

secrets.title: What Radegast wants
secrets.text: Radegast wants the Germans deflected north and the Hanseatic towns rotted by greed.

secrets.title: Radegast's disguises
secrets.text: Radegast poses as the pagan gods, and can dress Infernal power as Magic or Faerie: the auras of Rethra and Mount Radhost are really Infernal.

secrets.title: Radegast's pawns
secrets.text: Radegast's pawns are Imanitos Mendax, willingly; Roznov, unwittingly; a cult among the townsfolk of Holstein and the Slavic princes of Mecklenburg; and an Ash Gild-led war on the Norse it is planning.

secrets.title: Storyguide Notes
secrets.text: Might not given.

neighbours.name: The cult of Radegast
neighbours.summary: Worshippers of the Old Ways among the townsfolk of Holstein and the Slavic princes of Mecklenburg.

details.wants: (secret) the favour of their 'god' and power over their neighbours
details.offers: (secret) diabolic powers to its members

secrets.title: What the cult worships
secrets.text: Nobles and priests of the Holstein cities and the Mecklenburg princes who worship the demon Radegast believing it a god and receive diabolic powers.

secrets.title: The cult's high priest
secrets.text: Imanitos Mendax poses as the high priest of the cult of Radegast and gathers power among its members.

neighbours.name: The exsules of Fenistal
neighbours.summary: Nothing of them is known to the Order in 1220.

details.rules: (secret) two members always on guard; no outsider enters
details.wants: (secret) to stay hidden, steal the Order's advances and avenge themselves on the Tribunal
details.offers: (secret) shelter to failed apprentices; the old nature magic of Merinita

secrets.title: Who the exsules are
secrets.text: Fewer than a dozen self-styled exiles (exsules; one exsul) living at Fenistal in the Bohemian Forest: descendants of the losing faction of early House Merinita who rejected the Order after Myanar's death and keep a Hermetic-like tradition cut off from modern Magic Theory.

secrets.title: The exsules' learning
secrets.text: All the exsules know Parma Magica but imperfectly; most have studied from vis all their lives; the line bears Quendalon's curse; many have the blood of Merinita or of powerful magical spirits.

secrets.title: The exsules' nature magic
secrets.text: Heirs of Merinita's nature magic, many exsules have walked the Paths through the Forest. With little access to Hermetic grimoires their spells rouse nature's fury rather than strike directly.

secrets.title: What the exsules mean to do
secrets.text: The exsules mean to survive hidden, keep up with Hermetic advances by theft and spying, shelter failed apprentices, set the fae against the Order, and in the end take revenge on the Tribunal.

secrets.title: The exsules and Irencillia
secrets.text: The exsules count Irencillia their greatest enemy, though Irencillia knows nothing of them.

secrets.title: The exsules' household
secrets.text: The exsules keep no warriors and the barest servants, all former animals given human shape, which makes infiltration all but impossible; two members are always on guard.

secrets.title: The Huntress in the Wood
secrets.text: The Huntress in the Wood is the exsules' unwitting instrument.

secrets.title: Storyguide Notes
secrets.text: All have Weird Magic and Flawed Parma Magica; Poor Student is common; the line bears Supernatural Nuisance (Faeries) from Quendalon's curse; many have Mythic Blood from Merinita or from powerful magical spirits, and Ways of the Forest, Free Study and Study Bonus are common. Many may have overcome one or more Lesser Limits, and they may have taken in Diedne fleeing the Schism War, in which case they excel at spontaneous magic. Their spells should feel alien and frightening to a Hermetic magus.

neighbours.name: The Huntress in the Wood
neighbours.summary: A secret society within the Order, mostly of House Bjornaer's followers, devoted to preserving primal, nature-bound magic. Its members meet in secret wearing animal masks.

details.rules: Members meet masked as animals and keep one another's names secret
details.wants: Primal nature magic preserved; (secret) the Elder Gild and Irencillia in its hands
details.offers: Fellowship among the Order's wild-hearted magi

secrets.title: Who steers the Huntress
secrets.text: The Huntress in the Wood is unknowingly a pawn of the exsules of Fenistal, who have steered it since its founding.

secrets.title: Under the masks
secrets.text: With every face hidden, the Huntress's members do not know that not all of them are magi of the Order.

secrets.title: The Huntress's agenda
secrets.text: The agenda instilled in the Huntress in the Wood is to take over the Elder Gild and with it Irencillia.

neighbours.name: The Pomeranian shapeshifters
neighbours.summary: A close-knit but far from united community of mostly unGifted shapeshifters in Pomerania, long at feud with House Bjornaer, which no longer remembers why. They have factions and feuds of their own, and the most peaceable among them may treat with Prima Falke.

details.wants: Their old feud with Bjornaer settled on their own terms
details.offers: The shapeshifter's art, outside Hermetic tradition

secrets.title: Storyguide Notes
secrets.text: In the Crintera Schism arc they are admitted to House Bjornaer in 1227 and 1228 and mostly lean Wilderist, tipping the House's balance.

neighbours.name: The Rhine League
neighbours.summary: No such league exists in 1220.

details.wants: (secret) unjust tolls ended and the robber castles razed
details.offers: (secret) protection for merchants and lawful toll-takers

secrets.title: Storyguide Notes
secrets.text: If history holds: as toll stations grow to a dozen by mid-century and double in four years in the Interregnum of the 1250s, merchants and lawful toll-takers suffer, and Mainz and Worms found the Rhine League to protect their merchants; many cities, the princely nobles (the three archbishops and the Count Palatine) and lesser nobles join. It puts down unjust tolls by trade sanctions and by destroying robber-barons' castles, besieging or razing nearly a dozen and unseating several barons, and disbands after three years with its aims met. A formidable foe for any covenant that acts as or allies with a robber-baron: vast resources, a large army and God on its side.

neighbours.name: Lord Robert Schönburg's band
neighbours.summary: About a dozen malcontents and ruffians living in the ruins on Pfalz Island under Lord Robert Schönburg, taking river tolls that amount to piracy; Wolkan the branded thief is one of them.

details.wants: Tolls, by extortion if need be
details.offers: A living on the river for men nobody else will have

secrets.title: Robert's secret
secrets.text: Robert Schönburg is a diabolist.

neighbours.name: The harbour of Hamburg
neighbours.summary: The harbour of the town of Hamburg.

neighbours.name: The harbour of Lübeck
neighbours.summary: The harbour of the town of Lübeck.

neighbours.name: The harbour of Rostock
neighbours.summary: The harbour of the town of Rostock.

neighbours.name: The harbour of Bremen
neighbours.summary: The harbour of the town of Bremen.

neighbours.name: The harbour of Stettin
neighbours.summary: The harbour of the town of Stettin.

neighbours.name: The harbour of Baccharach
neighbours.summary: The harbour of the town of Baccharach.

neighbours.name: Pannonia's first site
neighbours.summary: Where Pannonia was founded, as a fortified covenant of House Tremere near the old meeting point of the Transylvanian, Greater Alps and Roman Tribunals. A powerful monastery was later built at the springs of the river the covenant drew its water from, and its Dominion destroyed the magic aura. Pannonia's magi scattered into camps, the first in the Tribunal to do so, and the magi of Old Histria now gather most of its old resources. The book gives no date and does not name the river or the monastery.

neighbours.name: Domostron's first site
neighbours.summary: The first home of Domostron, the covenant Tremere's Hermetic allies founded, later wrecked by raiders from the Theban Tribunal. The book gives neither date nor place; it is set here near the Theban border only as a guess.

neighbours.name: The Kal Valley and Lake Balaton
neighbours.summary: A secluded valley in the Tribunal's west, wild yet within reach of the great cities of Hungary and Italy. Hungarians use its name for the dullest place on earth, so a troupe can put anything there without disturbing the history it wants to keep. Close by lies Lake Balaton, the Tribunal's western gateway: never deeper than about three metres, ringed by rich farmland and on the main trade routes, so stories pass by its shores. One of chapter one's sites suggested for a new oppidum.

neighbours.name: Cakoc
neighbours.summary: A town near the Kal Valley with an odd pull on dragons. Saint George killed a black beast here long ago and so ended the custom of feeding it girls. In 1220 a green dragon lives in the nearby mountains; it scares the folk and takes their sheep but does little worse, so no one knows whether it is Infernal. It can talk, though it seldom bothers, beyond telling a shepherd to keep his dog close or lose it (see the Bestiary for the dragons). One of chapter one's sites suggested for a new oppidum.

neighbours.name: The Tomb of Attila
neighbours.summary: Somewhere under the bed of the Tisza lies Attila, king of the Huns, whom the Magyars count as their forefather and the founder of Buda. His people turned the river aside by a canal to bury him, his warriors cut themselves and rode about his body singing laments, and he was sealed in coffins of iron, silver and gold; then every labourer was killed so the place would be forgotten. Among his grave goods may be the Sword of Mars, a weapon fallen from the sky that let him scourge the world. One of chapter one's sites suggested for a new oppidum.

neighbours.name: Klingsohr's fields by the Tisza
neighbours.summary: The plain near the Tisza where the hidden bard Klingsohr wanders in peasant clothes, singing of Hungary's beauty to the empty fields. In 1207 the Margrave of Thuringia held a contest at Wartburg for the title of king of poetry, the losers to be put to death; Wolfram von Eschenbach beat Henry of Ofterdingen, who lamented that the one bard better than both was absent. Henry followed the songs that drift through Hungary's leaves, birds and storm clouds, which settle in the mind unbidden, and found Klingsohr, who cared nothing for prizes but came to save Henry's life. Crowned with bay by Wolfram, he had the death sentences lifted and foretold the Margrave's family's fate, which has come true in every point. He still foretells what is to come for anyone in need of it, or kind to him. One of chapter one's sites suggested for a new oppidum.

neighbours.name: The Sunken City
neighbours.summary: A Roman city that slid almost whole into the Black Sea, tied in ancient times to astronomers and their Mysteries. A covenant here would reach easily into Greek culture and trade, the Tribunal's heart and the lands east of the Order; many Black Sea islands nearby have strange myths of their own. On a modern map it is near Kavarna. One of chapter one's sites suggested for a new oppidum.

neighbours.name: The Isle of Achilles
neighbours.summary: A small Black Sea island where Achilles was buried. His temples are fallen, but since some mystical event in Roman times his spirit, Helen's and those of some of their followers dwell there. No woman may land, and men only by day, sleeping aboard ship if they stay longer; Achilles kills any visitor of Trojan blood, and Trojan princes settled as far as Rome and Britain. Fishermen use it as a safe anchorage in storms, if they dare. Tremere and their companions come to talk war with Achilles, calmer now than in life, and others ask Helen where ancient cities and temples lay; some scholars think the two are the heart of a mystery cult, though House Tremere has no record of one. Most tellers place Achilles' grave elsewhere, but the local folk and several ancient authors put it here. One of chapter one's sites suggested for a new oppidum.

neighbours.name: The Seventy-Seventh Island
neighbours.summary: The seventy-seventh island of the Black Sea lies under a darkness so thick a spoon would stand up in it. At its heart grow three reeds: in the middle one is trapped a maiden said to be the fairest in the world, and in the other two her handmaids. A witch guards them who must die the moment the Reed Maiden goes free. Only a steed raised on dragon's milk, fed live coals and given fire to drink can pierce the dark. One of chapter one's sites suggested for a new oppidum.

neighbours.name: Hungary
neighbours.summary:
The Magyar kingdom that holds the north of the Tribunal. Even beyond its borders, nobles of Hungarian blood and Hungarian quarters in the larger towns are common. King Andrew II rules it from a triangle of three court cities, Esztergom, Székesfehérvár and Veszprém, between which his court travels.

The royal lands are cut into 72 counties (megye), each run from a fortified town of earth banks, ditch and timber wall by a count (ispán) the king appoints; most counts hold several and send deputies, the curial counts, to the rest. A count lives on peasant rents and a third of his county's taxes, tolls and fines, and ranks with a bishop. Private castles are against the law and stone ones almost unknown. Frontier counts guard marches of log and earth barriers, with an empty border zone beyond, watched by Szekler and Pecheneg horse archers. The fringes have no counties: a voivode governs Transylvania, a ban governs Croatia, and the Dalmatian cities rule themselves by treaty with the Crown.

Andrew's 'new institutions' set twenty barons, chosen from the high nobility, above the counts: first the palatine, the judge royal, the ban of Croatia and the voivode of Transylvania, then the queen's and the chamber's masters, then the masters of horse, table and cup. He has given them huge royal estates, to arm them like western knights say his friends, to buy them and pay his crusade debts say his foes; since Hungarian land owes neither service nor tax, the gift goes further than any in France or Germany. Foreign settlements outside the counts' reach and the new class of freed royal servants have both cut into the counts' power.

Hungarians are reserved, courteous and stiff about the precedence birth gives them; they put the family name first and never talk of money, though no other subject is forbidden. Serfs are chattels; most free men are still bound to fight or work for a lord, and only the gentry and foreigners enjoy 'golden freedom'. Castle folk, castle warriors, the half-free royal serfs (udvornici) and the villages that owe the court one fixed trade or good (conditionarii) fill out the ranks, and hospites, guests such as the Saxons and Szeklers, live under their own laws. Any landholder counts as noble, and the gentry claim descent from 108 pagan chieftains of the conquest; the question of who is noble is still open, and the Golden Bull of 1222 may settle it on land, which would make most magi nobles without any oath. Villages are small and shifting, famine is almost unknown (the Quaesitors once checked for Hermetic meddling), and wheat is cheap.

The king's wealth rivals any in Christendom: if Andrew is as rich as his grandfather Béla, a third of it comes from reminting the coin each year at the one royal mint in Esztergom, the rest from tolls, the counties' taxes, the salt monopoly, the Saxons, the counts' yearly gift and the Slavonians. All mines are his, and he takes a tenth of the gold panned in Transylvania. Making metal or coin by magic robs that revenue and could bring a royal army down on an oppidum; the Order would not protect the culprit.

The Holy Crown. Hungarians hold that their crown, kept at Székesfehérvár, is a living Divine being linking God and man, ruling the land for the Virgin Mary, to whom Saint Stephen gave it; the kingdom is its body, all Hungarians are equal beneath it, and even a king may be lawfully resisted if he gives land to foreigners, meddles with others' land, brings in new kinds of justice, tramples the rights of natives or foreigners, or fails to defend the faith. Magi who stand against corrupt nobles have sometimes been helped by miracles. It is the Crown, not the king, that guarantees the magi their right to be judged by the Code; it intervenes rarely, but far more readily than any mortal king, and the Order dare not fail to police its own.

No witches. King Coloman the Learned decreed in the eleventh century that witches do not exist and none may be tried; the Quaesitors found no magus behind it. The Order's magic counts in law as the custom of an ancient people, so magi keep their own laws and judges, as Saxons, crusading orders and Pechenegs do. The great nobles know of magi and bring complaints to Redcap envoys in discreet town mansiones, but do not tell a magus from a village cunning man, so the Tribunal polices hedge wizards too; a hedge wizard in deep trouble may claim trial under the Ancient Custom, though the Code punishes harder than any Hungarian court.

The Church came with Saint Stephen as a tool of royal power and has stamped out paganism except among the Cumans. Every ten villages must build and furnish a church; laws on Christian conduct are harsh (talking in church earns a whipping), church lands are under royal protection, but paganism now draws only a fast, and Jews and Muslims serve the king in coinage and the treasury unhindered. Orthodox Romanians pay a sheep tax, the fiftieth, instead of tithe.

Horror seed: if history holds, the Mongols come in waves in the middle of the century, a horde that can only be fled, not beaten (see The Mongols).

links.note: an aždaja that sinks river boats on the upper Danube
a giant kept chained in a barrel in some king's palace

secrets.title: Vis at Hungary
secrets.text: Vis (each in its place): Gyogy-to (Ignem and Aquam), and Laniena's Aggtelek caves: Baradla (Imaginem and Muto), Dobsinska (Ignem) and Ochtinska (Rego).

neighbours.name: Gyogy-to
neighbours.summary: The biggest warm lake in Europe, beside Hévíz in the west of the kingdom. It yields both Ignem and Aquam vis, and as far as anyone knows, unlike many hot springs, it has no tie to Hell. There are traces of magic worked here by Romans and peoples before them. It lies just far enough from the Redcaps' road to Histria that no mansio stands here. A good site for a new oppidum; the book gives no aura.

neighbours.name: The Aggtelek Caves
neighbours.summary: A cluster of limestone caves in the hills of northern Hungary, beautiful beyond words, many of them with a Magic aura. Laniena stands at the mouth of the greatest, Baradla, and gathers vis from three of them. Some passages are thought to join one cave to another.

neighbours.name: Baradla Cave
neighbours.summary:
The largest and grandest of the Aggtelek caves, with the strongest aura of them, Magic 5: more than sixteen miles of winding galleries, dead ends and hidden chambers, crowded with columns, flowstone and dripstone streaked red, green and violet, some of it slumped as though the rock had softened like candle wax. Imaginem and Muto vis are both found here (Laniena's).

Only Lexander has explored it at length, and not all of it; he has warded every entrance he knows, because he turns vampires, werewolves and other captured horrors loose in the maze and sends his pupils after them.

neighbours.name: Dobsinska Cave
neighbours.summary: A cave further north, entered by a single sheer shaft the locals call the studena diera, the cold hole, for the cave is full of ice even at midsummer; few will climb down for fear of freezing in its depths. Laniena gathers Ignem vis here. The book gives its aura no number.

neighbours.name: Ochtinska Cave
neighbours.summary: One of the smallest caves and one of the strangest: its roof and walls sprout the 'flowers of iron', white tufts of stony needles like sea urchins. They are Rego vis, and also lesser enchantment vis that gives whoever bears one a personal Ward Against Faeries of the Earth (level 10, Penetration 10). Laniena's. The book gives its aura no number.

neighbours.name: The Estate of the Wizards
neighbours.summary: A mansio in Esztergom kept by House Mercere where travelling magi may stay: a graceful three-storey house like a Roman villa, older than any record, which its people say once stood outside the town; the city has grown round it, and it now sits in a ring of formal gardens. Nobles who have a grievance against magi bring it here, and when the king's judges and the magi's servants dispute who should try a case, they argue it out here. That magi deal with mundanes through servants is an old right the Holy Crown protects. Other mansiones, public and private, are scattered about the Tribunal.

neighbours.name: Kingdom of Hungary
neighbours.summary:
King Andrew (Endre, Andreas) II of the house of Árpád, who came home from the Fifth Crusade in 1218 deep in debt after raising the biggest crusading army ever seen. He is pushing through his 'new institutions', handing royal land and power to a new rank of barons to make the realm stronger in war; the reform is half done and may prove a mistake, and the old nobility resents both the barons and the king's freed royal servants. He farms out offices for cash and is thinking of auctioning the mint itself.

The king's own lands, the largest in the kingdom, are blocks of villages around royal manors (curtes), much of them royal forest kept by villages of foresters under a procurator. Unlike his nobles, the king does not split his lands among his sons. He is crowned by the Archbishop of Esztergom, at Székesfehérvár. The Church scolds him for his tolerance of Muslims, pagans and Jews. If history runs its course, his nobles force the Golden Bull on him in 1222.

neighbours.name: The Palatine of Hungary
neighbours.summary: First of the king's twenty barons, ranking with the judge royal, the ban of Croatia and the voivode of Transylvania above the rest. Barons are drawn from the high nobility and each holds at least one county; the king can remove one from office only by giving him something as rich. The book does not name the palatine.

neighbours.name: Archbishopric of Esztergom
neighbours.summary: Head of the Hungarian Church, enthroned in the basilica of Saint Adalbert, who baptised the royal house, on the crown of Esztergom's castle hill. He alone may crown the king. In name the Church stands with the Crown; in truth it is loudly critical of the king's leniency to Muslims, pagans and Jews, and the royal palace next door keeps the quarrel quiet. A Count of the Mint who keeps the Muslim minters would clash with him. The archbishopric is among the Church's richest landholders, and the bishops of the realm answer to it or to Kalocsa. Magi value the bishops of Veszprém as a weight against him.

neighbours.name: Archbishopric of Kalocsa
neighbours.summary: The second of Hungary's two archbishoprics, junior to Esztergom; part of the realm's bishops answer to it. With Esztergom it holds the largest church lands in the kingdom, and in theory it is a close ally of the king.

neighbours.name: Bishopric of Veszprém
neighbours.summary: The first bishopric of Hungary, founded by Saint Stephen. Its bishop has the old right to crown the queen; when another bishop crowned the present queen, the quarrel split the Hungarian Church until the Pope stepped in and confirmed Veszprém's right. Pannonhalma nearby is older and richer, so this is the poorest and weakest of the ancient sees, and its bishops usually stand close to the Order, which values them as a counterweight to the Archbishop of Esztergom.

neighbours.name: Bishopric of Pécs
neighbours.summary: One of the two bishoprics, with Oradea, whose lands are among the largest the Church holds in Hungary after the two archbishoprics.

neighbours.name: Bishopric of Oradea
neighbours.summary: A great landholding see (the book's Ordea), which keeps the Divine Dexter, Saint Stephen's mummified right hand, one of the kingdom's holiest relics.

neighbours.name: The Cathedral Chapter of Székesfehérvár
neighbours.summary: The richest and mightiest cathedral chapter in Hungary, in Saint Stephen's basilica. It guards the Holy Crown, a living Divine being, and the tombs of the kings. Its provost ranks with a count, and archdeacons run each of its counties for him.

neighbours.name: The Abbey of Pannonhalma
neighbours.summary: The biggest and wealthiest monastery in Hungary, a Benedictine house older than the see of Veszprém nearby and the mother house of many others; in 1200 it ruled 2,200 households. Its wealth is one reason Veszprém is poor.

neighbours.name: Esztergom
neighbours.summary:
The capital and biggest city of Hungary (the book's Esztergorm), an old camp of the Romans, of Attila and of the first Magyar king, where the roads to Kiev, Constantinople and Regensburg meet. The castle hill above the river holds the royal palace, built by western masons a few decades ago and the wonder of the realm, where foreign kings are always received, on the site of Saint Stephen's birthplace, so he is thought to watch closely over his heirs here; and the archbishop's basilica of Saint Adalbert. About 11,000 live in the town below, many of them foreign: craftsmen the king has hired and merchants, since the law makes every foreign trader offer his goods here first.

The Order's mansio, the Estate of the Wizards, stands here amid its gardens. Here too is the realm's only mint, whose Khwarezmian minters (the kaliz) are sharp at spotting false coin: magi who make coins of created silver are likelier to be caught here than in any other Tribunal.

Story seeds: the king, drowning in crusade debt, auctions the office of Count of the Mint each year, and magi could buy it openly or through a front, lawfully under the Code, though they must then hunt forgers and tax the miners; if they do not, a syndicate backed by Venetian bankers wins it, perhaps with House Mercere's domus magna behind it, and later the king splits the right among new mints at Csanád, Szerem, Buda and Zagreb. A faerie forger strikes coins bearing magi's sigils and oppida's marks. A royal coin inspector vanishes, perhaps tortured for his tests for forgery, and oppida race to find him for the king's favour or his secrets.

neighbours.name: Székesfehérvár
neighbours.summary: A city ringed by marsh, fortified by the first Magyar king, where Saint Stephen built a basilica and set a bishop; it has grown into the realm's centre of church learning, full of monasteries and churches and the largest cathedral school in the kingdom. Not the capital, but the city of ceremony: kings are always crowned here and, if they can be, buried here; pilgrimages begin here, the nobles meet here in their diets, and the regalia, the Holy Crown above all, are kept here, while the treasury proper is at Esztergom.

neighbours.name: Veszprém
neighbours.summary: The smallest of the three court cities, its castle older than the Magyar conquest; Saint Stephen's queen loved it, and he founded Hungary's first bishopric here. It is home to the college that trains the king's diplomats, whose library is one of the best in the land. If the Dragon War comes, dragons may try to burn it.

neighbours.name: The College of Veszprém
neighbours.summary: Where royal envoys learn their trade: the liberal arts and law are taught. With Mostre's school in Bosnia it is the nearest thing the Tribunal has to a university. Its library, among Hungary's finest, has served more than one magus, by lucky browsing or quiet borrowing.

neighbours.name: The Cathedral School of Székesfehérvár
neighbours.summary: The largest cathedral school in the kingdom.

neighbours.name: The Barons of Hungary
neighbours.summary: The twenty great officers of Andrew's new institutions, ranked by their titles above the counts and enriched with vast royal estates. The old counts and the gentry resent them, and the strain between old nobles and the king's newly freed men is growing; the quarrel may end in the Golden Bull.

details.wants: Royal land, office and precedence; the old nobility wants them curbed
details.offers: Armed retinues in the western style

neighbours.name: The Kaliz
neighbours.summary: The king's minters, all Khwarezmian Muslims (Hungarians call every minter kaliz), with some thirty villages of Turks and many Jews in royal service in trade, coinage and the treasury; the Lateran Council's rules against them are not enforced. The Church dislikes them, and magi who stamped coin by magic and let them go might please the archbishop.

details.wants: To keep the mint and the king's favour
details.offers: Skill at minting and at catching forgers

neighbours.name: Bulgaria
neighbours.summary:
The Second Bulgarian Empire, which in 1220 holds most of the Balkans between the Black Sea and the Morava, and Wallachia beyond the Danube too. Its capital is Tarnovo; Niš, Sredets and Silistra are its great cities, and Varna and Nesebar its ports. Its young tsar, Ivan Asen II, means to win back the old empire's glory, and if the saga follows history he will within ten years master Thrace, Macedonia and Epiros and push west into Serbian lands as far as Belgrade.

The land has always lived by its roads: the Danube and the Romanian plain carry trade from the Bosphorus to Central Europe, and so does the old highway by Adrianople, Plovdiv, Sredets, Niš and Belgrade. The fertile Danube lowlands in the north feed the empire; the Stara Planina runs across its middle; south of it lie the Sredets and Thracian plains, divided at the Gates of Trajan; and the Rila, Pirin and Rhodope ranges close the south.

Thracians, Romans, Goths and Slavs all settled it before Khan Asparukh's Bulgars crossed the Danube in 679 to 681 and built the First Bulgarian Empire, which lasted until Byzantium swallowed it in 1018. Krum took Hungary and Transylvania in 803 and died suddenly in 814 after beating two emperors and besieging Constantinople; Boris was baptised about 870 as Michael; Symeon took the title of tsar and gave the Church its own head in 926. Pechenegs, Magyars and Uzes followed. The brothers Teodor Petar, Ivan Asen and Kaloyan broke Byzantine rule in 1185, and Kaloyan, who reigned from 1197 to 1207, rebuilt the empire.

Bulgarians are stocky and dark, hard-working, tolerant and welcoming, steadier than the Serbs but stubborn fighters for a cause they think just. The men wear loose trousers tucked into tall boots, the women bright skirts, and both embroidered shirts with waistcoats or bodices.

Hermetically, three oppida lie here: Evredika, the scattered sancta of the Cult of Orpheus in the Rhodopes; Seuthopolis, the Quaesitors' town near the Shipka Pass, where the Tribunal meets; and Tablinum, the museum of regiones in the Danube delta. Gigas, the Theban Tremere lodge south-west of Sofia, lies just over the border.

Vis here (each in its place): the silivriak of the Rhodopes (Imaginem) and the bones of the Devil's Throat (Corpus), both Evredika's; Tablinum's Vim distillery; and Starosel's Terram and Herbam, which no oppidum holds. From a mountain eyrie the powerful aždaja Rabidanadas watches the demon Akgah's success in the Theban Tribunal and dreams of leading a band of aždaje against the Bulgarian kingdom.

links.note: the Bulgarian demon that wears a corpse
a four-eyed dog, born to hunt vampires

neighbours.name: The Danube Delta
neighbours.summary: Where the Danube meets the Black Sea it spreads into a wilderness of swamp, reed beds and marsh covering perhaps a thousand square miles, home to vast flocks of white pelicans and egrets. South of it the Dobrudja is a dry country of sandy steppe and low hills full of copper, poor in a drought but very rich where it can be watered. Tablinum hides among the dunes and wetlands of the coast.

neighbours.name: The Galleries of Tarnovo
neighbours.summary: The Roman city of Nikopolis ad Istrum stood some twelve miles north of Tarnovo until the Huns sacked it in 447. Legend says its people fled to Trapezitsa Hill carrying the city's riches, dug passages deep into the rock, and hid the hoard there behind deadly traps. Treasure seekers have hunted it ever since, and the townsfolk fear its traps and its curse.

secrets.title: The tunnel under a Tarnovo house
secrets.text: A Tarnovo man has found a tunnel beneath his house, and means to cheat whoever explores it of whatever gold they bring out.

secrets.title: Storyguide Notes
secrets.text: The Tarnovo man looks for foreign adventurers to explore his tunnel, since no local will go down.

neighbours.name: Baldwin's Tower
neighbours.summary:
A tower over Tarnovo's Frankish quarter, built to hold Baldwin, the Latin emperor of Constantinople, whom Tsar Kaloyan took in battle in 1205. Kept at first as a precious hostage, Baldwin ruined himself by courting Kaloyan's Cuman wife (or, some say, she charged him with rape when he refused her); he was bricked up inside, his cries carried over the quarter for months and then stopped, and the tsar told the pope he was dead.

Some say Kaloyan beheaded him and drank from his skull, and that his headless body, unburied, walks around the tower seeking vengeance on the Asens. At least one band of foreigners has tried to break in to free him, and failed: the tower cannot be forced.

secrets.title: Whether Baldwin lives
secrets.text: Others insist Baldwin still lives, a prisoner the present tsar keeps in the tower for some purpose of his own.

neighbours.name: The Stara Planina
neighbours.summary: The Old Mountains, Haemus to the ancients: a narrow chain running nearly four hundred miles west from the Black Sea through the heart of Bulgaria. High meadows feed sheep and cattle, beech woods cover the middle slopes, and the foothills are farmed. The range shields the Thracian Plain from the hard winters of the Romanian side.

neighbours.name: The Shipka Pass
neighbours.summary:
The best way through Bulgaria's mountains, near Seuthopolis. In the Order's early years Tremere himself fought a band of Theban magi here, and beside the battlefield lies a regio: some think it older than the fight and the place Tremere laid his ambush, others that the battle's strain threw some magus into Twilight and made it. For a long time afterwards House Tremere and the Theban covenants met in it to reflect and to sign treaties.

When House Guernicus took over the Tribunal site from the Praeco, and was asked to hold yearly Tribunals so that justice came quicker and trained apprentices were accepted sooner, the Quaesitors chose this regio: it was close to Seuthopolis and already had buildings. The full Tribunal every seven years is more a festival than a parliament, so the hall need not be large.

Groups of magi raise splendid temporary buildings on the valley's terraces, as lodgings, shops and places of amusement; new coloniae often first show themselves by pitching a tent on the Western Promenade, west of the hall, while visitors from other Tribunals, especially those with goods to sell, gather on the Eastern. Strolling the Promenades with friends, again and again with each circle one belongs to, is the great pleasure of a meeting, and newcomers are told to bring good boots. Redcaps race on foot between the two carved winged feet of Hermes that mark the regio's ends, and some take the races very seriously.

The Hall of the Tribunal is little more than an immense roof on plain columns of a Greek sort, a few carved in honour of magi who served the Order greatly, under a magically lit and richly decorated ceiling. Every magus of the Tribunal has a seat, in horseshoe rows around a dais, with room for a hundred more; on the dais stands the Praeco's oak throne, about whose making many tales are told. The servants of the visiting magi find the meetings full of romance, wagers, games and gossip.

levels.name: The Tribunal regio
levels.notes: The book gives no aura; 5 is the pack's. A terraced valley with the Hall of the Tribunal between the Western and Eastern Promenades, a giant winged foot of Hermes carved at each end.

neighbours.name: The Rila Mountains
neighbours.summary: The range south of Sredets, whose northern peak, Mount Vitosha, looms over the Sredets Plain; with the Pirin to the south it nearly meets the Stara Planina at the Gates of Trajan. Saint Ivan Rilski's monastery and his hermitage lie here, and the Seven Lakes high above.

neighbours.name: Ivan Rilski's Cave
neighbours.summary:
Saint Ivan Rilski (John of Rila), hermit, healer and mystic, who died in 946, lived twelve years in this cave, three in a hollow oak and seven on a high rock above it; the disciples his fame drew became the monastery that still stands. Cave, tree and rock each hold a Divine aura of 4, apart from the monastery's own Dominion aura of 3. The saint's uncorrupted body now lies at Tarnovo. Saint Ivan Rilski himself, Bulgaria's patron, is in the Bestiary.

Story seed: the monks speak for the nation's saint and sway the bolyeri, but before they grant a favour they may require the petitioners to repeat his life in little, twelve days in the cave, three in the oak and seven on the rock, while the saint tries the purity of their purpose. Those who pass may win the monastery's friendship; the same ordeal could serve as Initiation into a Holy Tradition of the saint.

neighbours.name: The Seven Lakes
neighbours.summary:
A chain of lakes high in the Rila Mountains, between about 6,900 and 8,200 feet, where faerie magic makes the water run from one lake to the next in no sensible order. The district has a Faerie aura of 3. A water-maiden vila, one of seven jealous sisters, lives in each lake (see the Bestiary); each offers a bather a faerie gift for a year and a day as her guest beneath the water, and must kill the guest on the last day.

Story seed: each sister's gift is a Minor Virtue with a Faerie Charm, and each can save the bearer from another sister's way of killing. Locals advise beginning at Babreka, whose gift sees through glamour and so defeats Dolnoto, the best illusionist; Dolnoto's gift, a lesser immunity to poison, is said to beat the sister who poisons her guests. Working out the order in which the water flows gives the order of the visits, and whoever wins all seven gifts is said to become the sisters' lord, owed their homage and obedience.

levels.name: The lake regiones
levels.notes: Each of the seven lakes has its own Faerie regio of 6, the home of its vila: top to bottom Salzata ('Tear'), Okoto ('Eye'), Babreka ('Kidney'), Bliznaka ('Twin'), Trilistnika ('Trefoil'), Ribnoto Ezero ('Fish Lake') and Dolnoto Ezero ('Lower Lake').

links.note: a template for the white ladies of the Tribunal

neighbours.name: Starosel
neighbours.summary:
A tomb temple of Bendis, the Thracian earth goddess, on the Thracian Plain, ringed by a wall of huge dressed stones carved with suns. The tomb is a mound reached by a broad stone stair to a landing; its cave-like door, framed in cut stone, opens on a plain antechamber and a splendid domed inner chamber painted with a bright frieze. It has a strong Magic aura of 6.

A fine site for a new oppidum, with ready-made and easily held walls, but it has a guardian: the place's genius loci, a hazy woman's shape of black earth and red clay with great power over earth, who can rouse the plants to help her and hates all change (see the Bestiary). Settlers must defeat or lastingly appease her; vis gatherers may strike a bargain to guard the temple for her in return. Starosel's genius loci, a magical spirit shaped like a woman of black soil and red clay with great power over earth and plants, guards the tomb temple and resists any change; settlers must master or pacify it for good, though vis gatherers may strike a bargain.

secrets.title: The genius and Bendis
secrets.text: Starosel's genius may or may not be the goddess once worshipped here; its Magic nature suggests not, and if so, something befell Bendis that settlers would be wise to learn first.

secrets.title: Vis at Starosel
secrets.text: Vis: Terram and Herbam, gathered within a few yards of the temple (the book gives no amounts).

neighbours.name: The Madara Plateau
neighbours.summary: A plateau that rises from the Thracian Plain in a sheer cliff more than three hundred feet high, long holy to the Bulgar shamans, with a Faerie aura of 3. At its foot a path climbs to a great cave under an overhang, green with plants and watered by a small spring: a natural theatre where the old Bulgars honoured three water nymphs.

links.note: a giant's mother on her hidden horse farm
the faerie horse starved on Nicoleta's farm

neighbours.name: The Madara Horseman
neighbours.summary:
Seventy-five feet up the Madara cliff a vast relief shows a rider spearing a lion under his horse's hooves, with an eagle flying before him and a hound behind: one of the Bulgar shamans' gods. Close to the carving the Faerie aura rises to 5.

The right faerie rite wakes the Horseman, and his horse, hound and eagle, which are part of his glamour, with him; the lion, a faerie in its own right, wakes too, and he must fight and beat it while he lives. He guards the local people he swore to protect and goes at once against whatever he judges their worst danger. Neither he nor the Lion (Faerie Might 20 or more each, the Lion's matching his) can be killed for good: the legend is so strong that other faeries of the region take up their glamour and they can be called again.

secrets.title: Storyguide Notes
secrets.text: Story seed: a bolyar the magi know begs them to shelter him from the Horseman, loosed on him, he says, by a faerie wizard. In truth he paid the wizard to raise the Horseman against his enemies, but the Horseman had heard his people's prayers and judged the bolyar's pride and ambition the region's worst threat. The wizard only failed to warn him. If the magi let things run their course, the Lion may interfere.

neighbours.name: The Rhodope Mountains
neighbours.summary:
A tangle of ridges and valleys in the south, with summer pasture above woods of pine and fir, and since antiquity the heart of the worship of Orpheus and of Zagreus (the Greeks' Dionysus), Thrace's two great gods. The magi of Evredika keep their scattered sancta here in caves, stout houses and hidden stone towers.

The silivriak, the Orpheus flower, grew from the singer's blood when the Maenads killed him: its pink bell flowers spring up anew each year even from a plant dried or scorched in a fire, and the year's first blooms give Evredika Imaginem vis. A vis-bearing flower is a Plant of Virtue that can be Enriched: write a poem each day for ninety days and recite them to it, then crush it and anoint three strings of an old-style lyre with its juice. The lyre gives its player Enchanting Music 3, effective only on the bereaved, which cannot be improved and replaces the player's own score; each broken string (on a botch, say) takes away a point for good.

neighbours.name: Gela
neighbours.summary: Evredika's: a small village in the central Rhodopes, the legendary birthplace of Orpheus. The Cult of Orpheus keeps a sanctum here, usually held by a magus with the Gentle Gift, who has a yearly grant of vis from the oppidum (as a Personal Vis Source) and in return must teach music and performance to anyone who asks. The village is now known for its musicians and draws pupils, Gifted and not, from the whole region. The magi of Evredika gather once a year in a green meadow near it, ringed by mountains, when the silivriak blooms.

neighbours.name: The Devil's Throat
neighbours.summary:
Evredika's: Diavolsko Garlo, a great cave into which a waterfall plunges far underground, said (though other places make the same claim) to be the door to Hades that Orpheus used to seek Eurydice. The Thracians once threw their dead kings down the fall to speed them to the afterlife. At the bottom the water pools in a still, dark lake, and on its shore, in the din of the falls, is the sanctum that by custom belongs to the oppidum's Tremere aedile. Magic aura 4.

The Orphic magi, who take Orpheus's descent as a journey of the spirit, care little for the site; they hold it for its history, and for the Corpus vis that now and then washes up on the lake shore as pieces of old skeletons.

neighbours.name: Perperikon
neighbours.summary:
Evredika's: a stone city on a hilltop in the eastern Rhodopes, once a great shrine of Zagreus, left empty by ordinary folk for centuries. The small town that has grown at the foot of the hill calls it the City of Ghosts; Evredika's covenfolk secretly live among the ruins and may account for some of the tales. Magic aura 3.

At its centre is an oval hall with a round altar on a stone dais: the oracle of Zagreus-Dionysus where Alexander learnt he would conquer Asia. A line of minor hedge wizards still takes auguries there the old way, pouring wine on the altar, setting it alight and reading the future in the flames; these priests are initiates of Divination and Augury who chiefly use pyromancy.

neighbours.name: The Rock Womb
neighbours.summary:
Evredika's: a cave near Perperikon shaped like a womb, with a carved altar at its far end. At noon a shaft of sun through a hole cut in the roof throws the shape of a phallus on the floor, and in January and February, with the sun low, on the altar itself; then the cave fills with a strong Magic aura of fertility (the book gives no number). Childless women come to lie with strangers here to conceive, and the children often carry magical blood.

A magus seeking the lost Fertility Magics may find Insight here, for instance by watching by magic the whole growth in the womb of a child conceived in the cave, which might show how to align children to Supernatural Virtues or Abilities.

neighbours.name: The Caverns of Seuthopolis
neighbours.summary: Seuthopolis's: under the fortified town lie the caverns of the old Thracian cult, with a Magic aura of 5 save in a few places. The magi use part of them for laboratories and libraries.

neighbours.name: The Crypt of the Martyred Virgin
neighbours.summary: Seuthopolis's: a vault in the caverns, hallowed by a martyred virgin's bones (Divine aura 3) and wrapped in layer on layer of magical defences. The Red and Black Libraries are kept here together, which troubles even magi who accept that they must exist; the Quaesitors answer that the vault cost a fortune and could not easily be built again.

neighbours.name: The Valley of the Thracian Kings
neighbours.summary:
The burial ground of the kings of ancient Thrace, close to Seuthopolis, their old capital, found four years ago by a Tremere necromancer then serving as a hoplite (the book gives no aura). House Tremere's necromancers were delighted; House Verditius wants to dig too, since the Thracians worshipped gods of the forge. Benilda, minding an old saying never to trust a happy necromancer, keeps everyone out for now, knowing Tremere will win in the end; she hopes to look first herself, or to steer who digs and why.

Saga seed: an excavation must be hidden from mundanes, get past cunningly trapped tombs, calm guardian spirits the magician kings left and the diggers wake, judge the magic items among the grave goods and whether they help Original Research, and learn of the Cabeiri, the Thracians' gods, and the powers they gave their servants, perhaps by journeys into the Magic or Faerie realms or by seeking Initiation into their Mysteries. In the Valley of the Thracian Kings a faerie calling itself Kabeiros, a tall brass man with a crab's claw for a left hand, is reviving the Cabeiri cult here, initiating Quaesitors' servants into Eyes of Theseus and the other cult Virtues.

secrets.title: The false Kabeiros
secrets.text: A strong local faerie, the false Kabeiros, is reviving the Cabeiri cult in the Valley of the Thracian Kings: a tall brass man with a great crab claw for a left hand, which serves him as smith's tongs and to punish the unjust. He courts the servants of Quaesitors, posing as the guide of kings and giver of justice.

secrets.title: The Kabeiros cult's degrees
secrets.text: The false Kabeiros's cult has four degrees (Interrogator, Invader, Observer, Liberator), all initiated in the valley on a holy day under a Vow to give fair and swift justice; they confer Piercing Gaze, Invasive Eyes, Bright Eyes and Eyes of Theseus, and he can take back Eyes of Theseus from the disloyal. He wants to teach Second Sight but has not yet stolen it from anyone.

secrets.title: Where the cult's idea came from
secrets.text: The false Kabeiros took the idea for his cult from a cult of servants at a Quaesitorial covenant who long ago worshipped Asmodeus as patron of prying; an Infernal scholar of the Black Library might trace it, and Asmodeus may punish the cult if he learns his idea was reused.

secrets.title: Storyguide Notes
secrets.text: The false Kabeiros: see the Bestiary.

neighbours.name: Tablinum
neighbours.summary:
On the Black Sea coast among the dunes and marshes of the Danube delta: to the eye only a palisaded village of a few grogs of Slav stock who fish from small boats amid clouds of pelicans and egrets. All that marks it is an Aegis of the Hearth of magnitude 8 round the palisade and a magic bell for calling the magi, which makes no sound except within Tablinum's regiones.

Here dozens of regiones lie on top of one another, each an exhibition hall: stone buildings joined by covered wooden walkways, vaulted halls under twisting brass chandeliers, narrow dark passages lined with scroll cases, alike in style but different in plan from level to level. The levels can be sensed but not crossed into by any path or ritual; one goes in only with an Arcane Connection and Leap of Homecoming or the like.
